Backups should be encrypted where appropriate, access-controlled, integrity-verified, versioned and protected against ransomware or unauthorized deletion. Recovery must be tested under an approved operational process; a backup existing does not prove it is restorable.

Define recovery point and recovery time objectives by data class and deployment context. Distinguish project revision recovery, evidence archive recovery, identity service recovery, plugin/build recovery and external connector recovery. The portable .gridforge package should remain recoverable without a live external service, subject to declared external evidence availability.

Incident response should include preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned. Containment actions must consider OT safety and availability. Isolating a gateway, disabling a plugin, revoking a credential or disconnecting a historian may affect plant visibility or engineering workflows; operational impact and compensating measures must be approved. Security incident handling must never automatically disable Protection, bypass interlocks or issue plant commands.

### P. Safety and security case evidence

V3 should support distinct but linked assurance cases:
- Cybersecurity risk assessment and security requirements.
- Functional safety hazard/risk assessment and safety requirements.
- Electrical Protection design/validation evidence.
- Process SIS lifecycle and verification evidence.
- Operational authorization and permit evidence.
- Software/product security lifecycle evidence.
- Project configuration integrity and change approval evidence.

Each claim must link to argument, assumptions, context, supporting evidence, evidence revision/hash, responsible author, independent reviewer, status and residual issue. A traceability graph can link a threat to a security requirement, control, verification result and residual risk; separately, a hazard can link to a safety function, SIL allocation, design, verification and validation. Cross-links show interaction but do not merge the two assurance claims.

Evidence status should distinguish planned, not assessed, partial, verified, failed, accepted with deviation, waived and superseded. A green dashboard or generated compliance matrix must not imply a certification. Independent assessment/functional safety assessment and competent-person approval remain external governance requirements where the applicable standard or regulation requires them.

### Q. Security and safety change management

Changes to software, dependencies, plugins, project files, topology, Protection settings, Control logic, SIS models, network conduits, identity policies, certificates, firmware, time sources and backup policies can affect security and safety differently. Change requests should identify change class, affected assets, threats, hazards, safety functions, security zones, operational dependencies, approvals, rollback and verification evidence.

A change to a security policy can lock out authorized operators or disable required monitoring. A patch can alter timing or resource use. A plugin can add a new network path. A relay setting change can affect fault clearing. A certificate rollover can interrupt communications. A time-source change can alter SOE correlation. Each change requires an impact assessment appropriate to its consequences.

Emergency changes require a controlled expedited path with scope, authorizer, rationale, compensating controls, expiry/review and retrospective review. Emergency status must not be a permanent bypass. Accepted baselines and issued evidence remain immutable; changed configurations create new revisions and linked supersession/impact records.

### R. Data classification, privacy and secure evidence exchange

Classify project and operational data by sensitivity and consequence: public, internal, confidential, restricted or a deployment-defined scheme. Classification should cover plant topology, equipment vulnerabilities, relay/PLC settings, network diagrams, credentials, supplier information, personnel identity, maintenance records, operational logs, incident reports and safety documentation.

Apply encryption in transit and at rest where appropriate, secure key management, least-privilege access, redaction, controlled export, recipient validation and retention/disposal policy. Metadata, thumbnails, logs, spreadsheet hidden sheets, embedded attachments and document properties can leak restricted information. Export should include a reviewable manifest of redactions and transformations.

The project package must not contain credentials, private keys, session tokens or unencrypted secrets. External evidence references must specify availability, access policy, integrity digest and whether the referenced content is embedded, cached or remote. A report or project export must not imply that a restricted external document is included when it is not accessible to the recipient.

### S. UI and human-factors requirements

Security and safety status must be explicit without creating alarm fatigue or implying false assurance. The UI should distinguish authenticated identity, active role, project scope, privilege elevation, authorization denial, pending approval, expired credential, untrusted signature, stale certificate, security warning, safety lifecycle status, Protection state and operational interlock status.

High-impact operations should show target, exact change, source revision, consequences, required approvals and recovery path before confirmation. Confirmation dialogs are not substitutes for authorization, technical validation or safety assessment. The UI must not use colour alone for security/safety state and must provide accessible descriptions, keyboard operation and clear focus.

Security settings should not be scattered across plugins or individual domain panels. Provide centralized policy and identity administration with domain-aware views. Show why an action is denied and the required approval path without disclosing sensitive policy internals to unauthorized users. Avoid exposing secrets in diagnostic messages or copied support bundles.

### T. Failure and degraded-mode semantics

Security infrastructure can fail: identity provider unavailable, certificate expired, signing service unavailable, trusted clock lost, policy service unreachable, plugin sandbox failure, backup unavailable, audit store full, external gateway disconnected or malware scanner unavailable. Each function must declare its fail-safe/fail-secure/fail-operational behavior according to the consequence and approved deployment policy; there is no universal fail-closed answer for every OT function.

For example, a report preview may be unavailable if authorization cannot be checked; an offline engineering project may remain readable under a documented local policy; a privileged configuration mutation may be blocked if identity assurance is unavailable; an already-running independent Protection relay must not depend on GridForge identity services to trip. The correct behavior is function-specific and must be documented in the deployment safety/security analysis.

Degraded modes must preserve evidence, identify unavailable controls and prohibit silent privilege escalation. Recovery after identity, clock, policy or audit outage should reconcile queued events and authorization state before resuming high-risk actions. Unknown command outcome remains unknown; security outage must not convert it into success or failure without feedback.

### U. Candidate standards and current-source findings

The following source checks were performed against official IEC, ISA and NIST publication pages on 2026-11-04. This is a research-level candidate map, not a BIS catalogue verification or conformance assessment.

1. IEC 62443-3-2:2020 defines the IACS System Under Consideration, zones/conduits, risk assessment, target security levels and documented security requirements. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/30727
2. IEC 62443-3-3:2013 addresses system security requirements and security levels, organized around identification/authentication, use control, system integrity, data confidentiality, restricted data flow, timely response to events and resource availability. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/7033
3. IEC 62443-4-1:2018 covers secure product development lifecycle requirements including security requirements, secure design/implementation, verification/validation, defect management, patch management and end-of-life. IEC currently lists Edition 2.0 under development with forecast publication in 2028; do not treat the future edition as published. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/33615
4. IEC 62443-4-2:2019 provides technical security requirements for IACS components. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/34421
5. ISA identifies ANSI/ISA-62443-2-1-2024 as the updated asset-owner security-program requirements, replacing the 2009 edition; verify corresponding IEC edition and national adoption separately. Source: https://www.isa.org/standards-and-publications/isa-standards/isa-iec-62443-series-of-standards
6. IEC TR 63069:2019 provides guidance for common application of IEC 61508 and IEC 62443 in industrial-process measurement, control and automation. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/31421
7. IEC 61511-1:2016+AMD1:2017 is the current consolidated IEC publication identified in the source check for process-industry SIS lifecycle requirements. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/61289
8. IEC 61508 Edition 3 parts appeared as 2026 pre-release/FDIS publications during the current research window, with voting period 2026-10-02 to 2026-11-13 and forecast publication 2027-01-22. They are not to be treated as final published editions as of this research date. The IEC page explicitly distinguishes functional safety scope from malicious-action cybersecurity requirements and points to IEC 62443 / ISO/IEC 27000 and IEC TR 63069 for coordination. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/117296
9. IEC 62351-3:2023 specifies TCP/IP security profiles using TLS, including TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 profiles, and security event handling. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/68410
10. IEC 62351:2026 SER is a series pack published 2026-07-30 and includes multiple parts with differing editions/years, including IEC 62351-8:2026 and IEC 62351-7:2025. A series pack is not a claim that every part has the same edition or scope. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/6912
11. NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 is the final OT security guide published September 2023. NIST published an initial public draft of Rev. 4 on 2026-09-21, with comments due 2026-11-30. Rev. 4 is a draft, not a final replacement at this research date; its stated updates include CSF 2.0 alignment, broader OT sectors, asset management, network monitoring and zero-trust-oriented system-management protection. Official sources: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/82/r3/final and https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/82/r4/ipd
12. IEC 61508-7:2026 PRV text notes that IEC 61508 does not itself provide normative requirements for malevolent action arising from security risk, and refers to IEC 62443 / ISO/IEC 27000 and IEC TR 63069 for coordination. Official source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/117302

Standards editions and status are time-sensitive. Before a V3 compliance baseline is approved, verify the official IEC/ISA catalogue, BIS adoption and amendments, licensing, applicable Indian legal/CEA requirements, contractual obligations and project-specific scope. No certification, SIL achievement, security level, BIS conformity or legal conclusion is claimed here.

### V. Candidate acceptance and usability scenarios

1. **UI-ACC-SEC-01** — A deployment threat model identifies assets, trust boundaries, entry points, threat actors, consequences, mitigations and residual-risk owners.
2. **UI-ACC-SEC-02** — Zones and conduits are defined for a selected system boundary with explicit permitted flows, protocols, identities and risk rationale.
3. **UI-ACC-SEC-03** — A plugin has a separate identity and declared capability set; installation does not silently authorize execution or network access.
4. **UI-ACC-SEC-04** — A plugin cannot mutate Core, access private persistence, read secrets or bypass Application authorization.
5. **UI-ACC-SEC-05** — A high-impact command is authorized at execution time against current actor, scope, target, project revision and policy.
6. **UI-ACC-SEC-06** — Authentication, authorization, engineering validation, Protection interlock, safety permit and command acknowledgement remain separate typed outcomes.
7. **UI-ACC-SEC-07** — An expired/revoked credential or unavailable identity provider blocks privileged changes according to the approved degraded-mode policy without disabling independent Protection operation.
8. **UI-ACC-SEC-08** — Break-glass access is time-bounded, purpose-bound, alerted and subject to retrospective review.
9. **UI-ACC-SEC-09** — A malicious or malformed .gridforge archive is rejected safely before project state changes or script execution.
10. **UI-ACC-SEC-10** — Project signature verification distinguishes valid, unknown signer, invalid, expired, revoked and unsigned states without implying engineering correctness.
11. **UI-ACC-SEC-11** — Configuration hashes and revision history detect changes and identify the approval record separately from integrity verification.
12. **UI-ACC-SEC-12** — A security policy or plugin update triggers an impact assessment for safety, timing, availability and engineering behavior.
13. **UI-ACC-SEC-13** — IEC 62351-capable communication adapter declares exact part/profile, TLS settings, identity, certificate lifecycle and failure behavior.
14. **UI-ACC-SEC-14** — A legacy unauthenticated protocol is confined to an explicitly assessed conduit with compensating controls and no implied end-to-end security.
15. **UI-ACC-SEC-15** — Security event records preserve source time, receive time, clock quality, actor, policy decision and tamper-evident audit provenance.
16. **UI-ACC-SEC-16** — Security monitoring or audit backpressure cannot silently overload or alter deterministic Protection/Control execution.
17. **UI-ACC-SEC-17** — A safety requirement and a cybersecurity requirement are separately traceable while their interaction and conflicting controls are linked.
18. **UI-ACC-SEC-18** — A dashboard cannot claim SIL achievement, IEC 62443 security level or certification from component presence or a completed template.
19. **UI-ACC-SEC-19** — A signed software/plugin/configuration update is checked for target, compatibility, approval, backup and rollback before deployment.
20. **UI-ACC-SEC-20** — A backup restore preserves project revision, evidence, signatures, security metadata and audit history or declares precisely what cannot be restored.
21. **UI-ACC-SEC-21** — A security incident containment action exposes operational impact and cannot automatically disable Protection, bypass interlocks or issue plant commands.
22. **UI-ACC-SEC-22** — A certificate, time-source or identity outage produces the declared function-specific degraded mode and an auditable recovery path.
23. **UI-ACC-SEC-23** — A controlled export redacts restricted data, secrets and sensitive metadata and records recipient, policy and transformation.
24. **UI-ACC-SEC-24** — Security, functional safety, Protection and operational authorization evidence can be reviewed independently and linked through a common assurance trace without being conflated.

### W. Open decisions, dependencies and gates

Open decisions include: supported deployment profiles and threat-model boundaries; security-zone reference architectures; target security-level methodology and ownership; identity provider and offline identity policy; role/attribute model; privileged access and break-glass governance; project signing and key trust model; plugin signing, sandbox and capability policy; software supply-chain and SBOM format; vulnerability disclosure and patch SLA; build/release signing and provenance; device configuration/firmware deployment boundary; protocol security profiles; certificate and trusted-time lifecycle; security event retention and tamper evidence; backup encryption and immutable storage; incident response and OT contingency ownership; data classification and redaction; functional safety scope and safety lifecycle support; SIL evidence model; independent assessment and competence requirements; safety/security coordination process; Indian legal/CEA/BIS applicability; and criteria for any future certification claim.

Dependencies: 8I-10 UI/UX gates; 8I-12 cross-domain traceability; 8I-21 diagnostics/events; 8I-22 collaboration/change control; 8I-23 persistence/recovery; 8I-24 data exchange; 8I-25 standards/compliance traceability; 8I-26 solver governance; 8I-27 simulation runtime; 8I-28 through 8I-31 equipment/network architecture; 8I-32 calibration/uncertainty; 8I-33 signal/measurement infrastructure; 8I-34 Protection/Control signal consumers; 8I-35 operational lifecycle; 8I-36 event/alarm/SOE/historian/audit; 8I-37 reporting/evidence; and 8I-38 asset lifecycle/maintenance/condition monitoring.

UI-GATE-02 Project/session, UI-GATE-03 Diagnostics, UI-GATE-04 Accessibility/platform, UI-GATE-05 Display/performance, UI-GATE-06 Cross-domain trace and UI-GATE-07 Scope/priority remain open. This entry closes no gate. Security architecture, functional safety scope, deployment boundaries, legal obligations and assurance claims require independent review by cybersecurity, functional safety, Protection, Control, operations, quality and legal specialists before approval.

### X. Frozen invariants and research boundary

- Cybersecurity, functional safety, electrical Protection, process SIS, Control, operational authorization and safety permits are related but distinct assurance disciplines.
- GridForge is not presumed to be a certified safety system, safety PLC, protective relay, industrial firewall or security monitoring appliance.
- Core remains authoritative for engineering/domain facts and Protection/Control semantics; security policy cannot rewrite domain truth or bypass engineering validation.
- Authorization is enforced at the Application command boundary at execution time; UI visibility is not an authorization control.
- Authentication, authorization, validation, interlock, permit, dispatch, acknowledgement and physical feedback remain distinct outcomes.
- Plugins are separate trust principals, constrained by declared capabilities and isolation; plugin code cannot directly mutate Core or access secrets.
- Project files and external inputs are untrusted at import boundaries; no project-supplied scripts/macros execute on open.
- Configuration integrity, provenance, approval and engineering correctness are separate claims.
- Security controls must be assessed for effects on safety, deterministic timing and OT availability; safety concerns do not create blanket cybersecurity exemptions.
- Protection and process SIS execution remain independent of GridForge identity, reporting, plugin, historian or cloud services.
- IEC 62443, IEC 61508, IEC 61511, IEC 62351, IEC TR 63069 and NIST OT guidance are candidate references subject to edition, applicability and national-adoption verification.
- Draft/pre-release standards are clearly labelled and are not treated as final published requirements.
- Security event monitoring and audit do not become a competing alarm/SOE/Protection execution engine.
- High-impact changes, updates, emergency access and incident containment require explicit authority, traceability and recovery planning.
- V2 main remains unchanged. V3 proposals require review and approval before implementation.

**Scope boundary:** research register only. No authentication provider, authorization engine, policy service, plugin sandbox, project-signing system, secure communications adapter, SBOM pipeline, vulnerability scanner, incident-response service, safety lifecycle engine, SIL calculator, security UI, source code, runtime behavior, benchmark, test or CI was implemented or executed. This entry performed targeted source checks for selected IEC, ISA and NIST publications but did not complete BIS catalogue verification, a deployment threat assessment, a functional safety assessment, an IEC 62443 gap assessment or any certification/conformity assessment. V2 main remains unchanged.


## 8I-40. Proposed V3 engineering data architecture, canonical schemas, semantic versioning, units, provenance and compatibility (2026-11-04)

### A. Research objective and governing principles

V3 requires a coherent engineering-data architecture so every domain, plugin, solver, report, exchange adapter and UI interprets the same engineering fact with the same type, identity, unit, semantics, provenance and revision context. A numerically valid value with the wrong physical dimension, reference frame, phase basis, operating condition, source or validity interval is not a valid engineering input.

The architecture should establish canonical domain-owned data contracts; stable object identity separate from tags and reference designations; typed quantities with dimensions, units, scale/basis and uncertainty; explicit topology, terminal, phase, polarity, direction and coordinate-frame semantics; versioned schemas and controlled migrations; provenance and lineage; separation of canonical internal models from external exchange formats; reproducible historical interpretation; validation at trust and domain boundaries; and controlled extension without allowing plugins to redefine shared semantics.

The canonical model is not one universal JSON document, global schema, database layout or exchange standard. It is a governed family of domain schemas with shared identity, quantity, time, provenance, validation, versioning and reference conventions. Domain owners retain authority over their facts; shared infrastructure supplies reusable primitives and policy.

### B. Data ownership and bounded contexts

Data ownership follows the frozen architecture:
- Core owns canonical engineering/domain facts: equipment, terminals, topology, signal semantics, Protection/Control domain facts, validation, study abstractions and engineering results.
- Application owns controlled mutation, commands, transactions, revision management, migration orchestration, event publication, project lifecycle and cross-domain coordination.
- UI owns interaction state, layout/projection and presentation formatting, not engineering truth.
- Plugins own extension-specific models through public contracts and declared namespaces; they cannot redefine or directly mutate Core-owned facts.
- Exchange adapters map external data to/from canonical contracts and report fidelity, losses, assumptions and unsupported constructs.
- Persistence owns durable serialization and recovery mechanics without becoming a second domain authority.
- Reporting consumes immutable revision-bound data packages and does not silently change canonical source data.

Each bounded context should publish a contract catalog: concepts, identifiers, schema namespace, owners, invariants, commands/events, read models, extension points, version policy, migration policy and external mappings. Cross-domain references use stable identifiers and typed relationships, not display labels or copied mutable records.

Avoid a shared mutable object model that causes unrelated domains to depend on each other's internals. Shared primitives must be small, semantically precise and versioned. A physical quantity is reusable; a protection pickup setting, motor thermal parameter and cable ampacity remain domain-specific concepts even if all serialize as numeric quantities.

### C. Canonical identity, references and designation

Every persistent engineering entity needs a stable, globally unique identity within a documented namespace strategy. A UUID/URI-like identifier is a candidate implementation, but the contract must specify scope, generation, collision handling, import behavior, merge behavior and identity preservation.

Keep separate:
- Internal stable object ID.
- Human-readable tag or equipment designation.
- Structured reference designation (e.g. IEC 81346 aspects).
- Manufacturer/model/serial identifiers.
- External system identifiers (ERP/EAM/CMMS/SCADA/IED).
- Display name and localized label.
- Functional location and installation position.
- Historical aliases and retired identifiers.

A tag is not a primary key. Tags may be renamed, reused under controlled rules or duplicated in different scopes. External IDs are not automatically globally unique. Import mapping records source system, source key, mapping decision, confidence and provenance.

Reference designation should be structured and aspect-aware, not one opaque string. IEC 81346 supports structuring principles and unambiguous reference designation across technical domains; ISO/TS 81346-101:2025 gives power-supply-system application guidance. Preserve user-defined designation schemes and map them explicitly; do not force one project convention into Core identity.

### D. Schema organization and canonical contract registry

Define schemas by domain and contract purpose, with stable namespace and schema identifier. A schema record should include namespace and canonical schema ID; name and definition; version and compatibility declaration; owner and approval status; effective date and deprecation/sunset status; dependencies; validation rules and semantic constraints; serialization profile and canonicalization rules; migration path and supported source versions; standards/term mappings and licensing constraints; examples/conformance fixtures; and change history/approval evidence.

A registry distinguishes draft, proposed, approved, deprecated, withdrawn and unsupported schemas. Published schemas are immutable; a changed contract receives a new version or identifier. Do not mutate a released schema in place if it changes interpretation or validation.

Schema definition language and runtime model are separate decisions. JSON Schema 2020-12 is a candidate for structural validation of JSON serialization; it does not by itself express all electrical, temporal, dimensional, topology or safety invariants. Domain validation remains owned by domain validators and explicit semantic constraints. A JSON Schema format annotation must not be assumed to enforce a domain rule unless validator configuration explicitly asserts it.

### E. Data types and semantic precision

Use explicit types rather than primitive strings/numbers for engineering meaning. Candidate shared types include EntityId, ProjectId, RevisionId, SchemaId, ExternalReference; Quantity, UnitCode, DimensionVector, Scale/Basis and QuantityKind; EngineeringValue with status/source/uncertainty/conditions; Timestamp, TimeInterval, ClockQuality and ValidityInterval; Phase, PhaseSet, SequenceComponent, Polarity and Direction; Coordinate, CoordinateFrame, ReferenceFrame and Orientation; TerminalId, ConnectionId and TopologyRevision; Measurement, QualityState and CalibrationReference; stable-code Enumeration; ProvenanceReference and EvidenceReference; SourceRevision; Diagnostic and ValidationFinding; Approval and ChangeRecord.

Do not use one generic numeric value contract for all engineering quantities. Complex impedance, phasor, vector, matrix, curve, waveform, state, categorical rating and scalar measurement are different types. Nullable fields must distinguish absent, unknown, not applicable, not measured, invalid, withheld and intentionally cleared where those states matter.

Enumerations need stable machine codes and human-readable labels. Never persist localized display strings as canonical enum values. Unknown future enum values require explicit compatibility behavior; silently mapping an unknown protection mode or phase state to a default is unsafe.

### F. Quantity, dimension and unit model

Every physical quantity should carry or reference quantity kind/semantic definition; numerical magnitude and representation (integer, decimal, rational, floating, complex, vector, matrix or time series); unit code and unit definition/version; dimension vector or equivalent semantics; scale, prefix and conversion policy; reference conditions where relevant; sign convention, orientation or reference frame where relevant; precision, resolution and rounding policy; and uncertainty/quality/provenance where applicable.

Store a canonical value using a documented canonical-unit policy per quantity kind, or preserve source value with explicit unit and reproducible conversion. Do not mix approaches without an explicit field contract. Preserve original source magnitude/unit and conversion provenance where source fidelity matters.

Dimensional analysis must reject incompatible operations: adding voltage to current, comparing absolute temperature with temperature difference without correct semantics, combining values with incompatible reference frames, or using hertz as radians per second without conversion. Dimensional correctness is necessary but insufficient: torque and energy share dimensions but have different quantity kinds; active and apparent power are not interchangeable.

Support affine units and offsets correctly. Celsius/Fahrenheit absolute temperature is not interchangeable with temperature interval/difference. Gauge and absolute pressure require explicit reference. Logarithmic quantities (dB, dBm, dBµV) require reference quantity, impedance/reference and operation semantics. Per-unit values require base quantities and base context; 1.05 pu is incomplete without applicable voltage/power base and phase/line convention.

### G. Electrical engineering quantity semantics

Electrical domains require more than SI dimension:
- Voltage/current: RMS/peak/instantaneous, phase-to-neutral/phase-to-phase, line/phase, AC/DC, polarity and direction.
- Power: active/reactive/apparent, sign convention, import/export, phase basis and measurement interval.
- Frequency/angle: hertz vs angular frequency, electrical vs mechanical angle, degrees/radians, phase reference and wrap convention.
- Impedance/admittance: complex representation, frequency, sequence, phase-domain or equivalent basis.
- Energy: integration interval, meter direction, import/export and reset/rollover behavior.
- Temperature: sensor type, location, compensation, ambient/reference conditions and calibration.
- Pressure/flow/level: absolute/gauge, mass/volume, reference density/conditions and direction.
- Mechanical rotation: speed, torque, inertia, shaft reference and sign.
- Thermal quantities: heat flow, thermal resistance/capacitance, temperature difference and boundary conditions.

Three-phase quantities need explicit phase set, phase order, neutral/earth reference, symmetrical-component sequence, vector group, connection type and line/phase convention. Phasors should carry complex value, frequency, reference time, phase reference, RMS/peak convention and quality. A magnitude without its phase/basis is insufficient to reproduce a study input.

Per-unit data must carry explicit base context: Sbase, Vbase, derived Ibase/Zbase, phase/line basis, frequency and transformer-side/base conversion. A per-unit value without base reference is incomplete for calculations. Transformer ratio/vector-group mapping cannot be inferred from a display string.

### H. Precision, numeric representation and numerical stability

Choose numeric representation by domain need. Decimal/fixed-point may suit exact decimal nameplate/settings and commercial values; binary floating point suits many numerical solvers; rational representation may suit exact ratios/unit definitions; complex and array types are required for network studies. Contracts state accepted ranges, precision, rounding, overflow and NaN/infinity handling.

Do not silently round a protection setting, CT ratio, instrument scaling, equipment rating or accepted nameplate value to fit a UI widget. Distinguish display precision from stored precision and solver precision. Preserve source resolution and uncertainty. Avoid binary floating-point equality for identity or engineering acceptance decisions; use domain-specific tolerance and comparison rules with units and rationale.

Numerical solver outputs include solver/model version, input snapshot identity, numerical options, convergence status, residual/quality indicators, precision mode, execution backend and warnings. GPU/NPU/CPU execution differences must not change result semantic type or provenance. A display-rounded result must not be reused as solver input.

### I. Engineering value status, provenance and confidence

A value is not fully described by magnitude. Model status explicitly: design/specified; calculated/derived; manufacturer guaranteed; manufacturer published/catalog; nameplate/as-built; factory test; site test/field measured; commissioned/accepted; calibrated measurement; estimated/assumed; inferred/model-generated; maintenance observed; imported/externally supplied; unknown/not available/not applicable/invalid.

Record source identity, source document/revision, author or instrument identity, observation/creation time, received time, approval, transformation, calibration, uncertainty and applicable operating conditions. Confidence/quality is not a substitute for provenance. A model-generated estimate must never silently overwrite measured or nameplate data.

When sources conflict, preserve competing assertions and record resolution decision, authority, rationale, reviewer and effective scope. Do not silently select the newest timestamp or highest numerical precision. Source precedence is domain-specific and documented.

### J. Provenance, derivation and data lineage

A derived value identifies inputs, transformation/activity, model or formula version, parameters, execution context, actor/service, time, source revision and output. A provenance graph links source entities/documents/measurements; import/conversion/calibration activities; engineering agents/tools; canonical facts; study snapshots and solver runs; Protection/Control evaluation inputs and decisions; report data packages/rendered artifacts; and export mappings/recipients.

W3C PROV-DM/PROV-O are candidate conceptual models for entity/activity/agent and derivation relationships. GridForge should adopt only concepts needed for engineering provenance and keep domain semantics explicit. A generic RDF graph or ontology must not become a required runtime dependency merely because it offers a provenance vocabulary.

Lineage is revision-aware and immutable for accepted results. A source change identifies affected descendants but does not mutate historical results/reports. Provenance distinguishes derivation, reference, correlation, validation, approval and supersession; these are not interchangeable edges.

### K. Time semantics and temporal validity

Engineering data needs distinct temporal concepts: valid time (when a fact is true in the represented system); transaction/recorded time (when GridForge learned/stored it); measurement/sample time; receive time; processing time; approval/effective time; simulation time (separate from wall clock); and expiry/validity interval.

Use explicit timezone/offset policy and preserve source time and clock quality. Never assume local machine time is authoritative. Time intervals define inclusive/exclusive boundary semantics and behavior for unknown endpoints. Historical values/configuration should be queryable “as known at” and “valid at” distinct instants where bitemporal semantics are needed.

Calibration validity, maintenance state, relay configuration effective period and measurement freshness are domain-defined validity concepts, not generic timestamps.

### L. Relationships, graph identity and reference integrity

Represent relationships as typed entities or typed links with stable IDs when they have lifecycle, attributes, provenance, direction, validity, approval or external mapping. Examples include electrical connection, containment, installation, measurement association, control dependency, Protection zone membership, ownership, derived-from, calibrated-by and referenced-by.

A generic parent ID is insufficient to represent multiple independent structures. Electrical topology, functional hierarchy, physical installation, instrumentation loop, signal routing, Control dependency, Protection zone, asset hierarchy, document structure and project ownership remain distinct graphs. A node may participate in several graphs without merging their semantics.

References declare expected target type and cardinality. Referential integrity identifies missing, ambiguous, dangling, cross-project, wrong-type, stale or unauthorized references. Import/merge preserves graph identity and avoids accidental duplication. Relationship deletion has explicit semantics for dependent objects and evidence.

### M. Schema evolution and semantic versioning

Schema versioning communicates structural and semantic change. Candidate policy:
- Major: incompatible meaning, required field change, identifier semantics change, unit/dimension interpretation change, invariant change or removal of supported behavior.
- Minor: backward-compatible addition with defined defaults/unknown handling and no reinterpretation of existing values.
- Patch: correction that does not alter data interpretation or validation semantics; otherwise it is not patch-only.

Version numbers alone are insufficient. Every schema release declares compatibility direction/scope: reader compatibility, writer compatibility, round-trip preservation, forward-field handling, downgrade loss and migration availability. Define whether unknown fields are preserved, rejected or quarantined; do not discard silently where round-trip fidelity matters.

Avoid implicit “latest schema” interpretation. Persist schema ID/version with project or object payload as required. Project manifest version is not a substitute for individual domain contract versions. Plugin contract version, API version, event version, serialized schema version, domain model version and external standard edition are distinct.

### N. Migration, downgrade and compatibility strategy

Migrations are explicit, deterministic, ordered and versioned. A migration package identifies source/target schema, migration implementation/version, preconditions, transformations, loss policy, validation results, provenance and rollback/backup requirement.

Separate lossless structural migration; semantic migration requiring assumptions/user decisions; external format conversion; project package migration; domain model migration; API/command/event migration; report/template migration; and plugin compatibility migration.

Never invent engineering values to satisfy a new required field. If a value cannot be established, preserve unknown/needs-review and produce a diagnostic. If a model changes units or semantics, require explicit conversion with source/target dimensions, bases, reference conditions and provenance.

Downgrade is potentially lossy export, not reverse migration. Produce a loss report identifying unsupported fields, relationships, precision, semantics, evidence and extension payloads. Never claim round-trip equivalence unless verified for the defined profile.

### O. Unknown fields, extension namespaces and forward compatibility

Unknown data handling is context-specific. For read-only viewers, safe preservation of unknown extension fields may be preferable to rejection; for high-consequence commands and solver inputs, unknown semantics must be rejected or quarantined rather than guessed. A project editor must not discard unknown fields merely because its version does not understand them.

Use namespaced extension payloads with publisher/owner, schema ID/version, declared capabilities, validation rules and migration policy. Extension data cannot shadow/override canonical Core fields. A plugin may add an extension through an explicit contract, but cannot redefine rated voltage, terminal, phase or ProtectionDecision semantics.

Provide round-trip preservation acceptance scenarios for unknown fields at persistence/exchange boundaries. Arbitrary extension blobs must not bypass schema validation or unbounded storage limits.

### P. Canonical serialization, persistence and deterministic representation

The frozen .gridforge ZIP structure remains manifest.json plus canonical project.json for canonical project facts and saved scope. This section does not authorize a new package root or competing database truth. The manifest identifies package format version and project identity; project/domain objects identify schema contracts as required.

Canonical serialization rules specify encoding, key/array ordering where semantically relevant, numeric encoding, Unicode normalization, null/absent semantics, date-time representation, enum codes, unit codes, stable reference format, extension handling and hash scope. Canonicalization for hashing/signing is explicit and versioned; ordinary JSON byte equality is not semantic equality.

Do not use serialization hash as sole identity of an engineering entity. Hashes identify content under a canonicalization algorithm; stable IDs identify entities across revisions. Content-addressed blobs may optimize storage but do not replace project/entity identity or provenance.

Atomic save, recovery, migration, signature and package-integrity requirements from 8I-23 and 8I-39 remain applicable. Serializer must not serialize UI scene objects, live Qt objects, caches, transient handles, open file descriptors or process-specific runtime state as canonical engineering facts.

### Q. API, event and command contract evolution

Commands, domain events, read models and integration APIs need separately versioned contracts. Event schemas are immutable once published; corrections use new events or explicit amendment/supersession records. Consumers declare supported event versions and unknown-event behavior.

A command should include command ID/type, target identity, actor/service identity, requested operation, source revision, expected version/ETag, idempotency key, correlation/causation IDs, authorization context, reason and expiry where applicable. These are not interchangeable with serialized entity fields. Command versioning preserves authorization and domain validation boundaries.

API evolution should prefer additive fields and new endpoints/operations where semantics change. Breaking changes require explicit version/deprecation policy and supported overlap period. UI clients/plugins must not infer contract semantics from internal class names or Python import paths.

### R. External standards, dictionaries and interoperability mappings

External standards are semantic authorities only within defined scope and edition. Mapping to an external schema does not make it the canonical GridForge model. Maintain mapping profiles with source/target schema versions, rules, code lists, units, reference designation, cardinality, loss report and limitations.

Candidate references:
- IEC 61360 / IEC CDD for common data element definitions, classifications and units for product/component data.
- IEC 81346-1 and IEC 81346-2 for structuring principles/reference designation; ISO/TS 81346-101:2025 for power supply system application.
- IEC 61970-301 CIM for power-system semantics and application-independent exchange.
- IEC 61850-6 SCL for substation IED/system configuration exchange; IEC TS 61850-6-3:2025 for machine-processable SCL validation rules; IEC TR 61850-90-30:2025 for function modelling in SCL.
- ISO 10303 STEP for product data representation/exchange and application protocols.
- ISO 80000 series and BIPM SI Brochure for quantities and units.
- UCUM for machine-readable unit codes where suitable.
- W3C PROV-DM/PROV-O for provenance concepts.
- JSON Schema 2020-12 for structural JSON schema validation.

Each mapping identifies normative vs informative use, edition/status, licence, applicable domain, mandatory/optional fields and extension policy. Standards-based dictionaries may contain overlapping terms; local definitions preserve source term, identifier, edition and mapping rationale. Do not copy licensed dictionaries into the repository or ship their content without confirming rights.

### S. Standards source check and edition/status observations

Targeted official-source checks were performed on 2026-11-04. These are candidate reference findings, not a complete standards catalogue or BIS verification.

1. BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition, current page lists Version 4.01 revised June 2026 and Version 3.02 revised August 2025; use the current maintained brochure, not an assumed frozen 2019 PDF. Source: https://www.bipm.org/en/publications/si-brochure/
2. ISO 80000-1:2022, Edition 2, provides general concepts for quantities, systems of quantities, units, symbols and coherent unit systems. Source: https://www.iso.org/standard/76921.html
3. UCUM specification version 2.2 is dated 2024-06-17 and describes a code system for units used in science, engineering and business. Source: https://ucum.org/ucum
4. IEC 61360-2:2012 corrected version 2025-03 provides an EXPRESS dictionary schema and computer-sensible representation/exchange of data element types; IEC 61360-7:2024 provides a cross-domain dictionary of generic concepts. Sources: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/5381 and https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/72956
5. IEC 81346-1:2022 establishes structuring principles and unambiguous reference designation rules across technical areas; it adds a type aspect and information models. Source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/64021
6. ISO/TS 81346-101:2025 gives guidelines and requirements for applying the 81346 series to power supply systems. Source: https://www.iso.org/standard/81285.html
7. IEC 61970-301:2020 Edition 7.0 describes CIM semantics for application-independent exchange between energy management systems; source page lists model content IEC61970CIM17v38. Verify later lifecycle updates and national adoption before selecting a profile. Source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/62698
8. IEC 61850-6 consolidated version IEC 61850-6:2009+AMD1:2018+AMD2:2024 CSV is Edition 2.2 and specifies SCL for IED capabilities/configurations, communication system configuration, substation/function structures and relationships. Source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/103863
9. IEC TS 61850-6-3:2025 defines machine-processable OCL rules for validating IEC 61850 XML-based files at engineering stages. Source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/79695
10. IEC TR 61850-90-30:2025 describes function modelling in SCL, including function decomposition/classification, links to logical nodes/IEDs and information flows. Source: https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/94414
11. ISO 10303-1:2024 Edition 3 defines STEP series architecture and product information representation/exchange principles, including EXPRESS and application protocols. Source: https://www.iso.org/standard/83105.html
12. W3C PROV-O is a W3C Recommendation (2013) expressing the PROV data model using OWL and supporting interoperable provenance descriptions across systems. Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/
13. JSON Schema official specification page identifies 2020-12 as the current published specification at the time of source check. An October 2026 Internet-Draft for a subsequent JSON Schema specification exists but is not a final standard and must not be treated as published normative version. Sources: https://json-schema.org/specification and https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-jsonschema-json-schema/

### T. Validation architecture and data quality

Validation is layered:
1. Serialization/parse: encoding, syntax, archive safety and resource bounds.
2. Schema: required fields, primitive types, enum codes, cardinality and structure.
3. Semantic: quantity kind, dimensions, unit, reference frame, phase/basis and temporal meaning.
4. Referential: IDs, relationship target types, project scope and graph consistency.
5. Domain invariants: electrical topology, Protection/Control constraints, equipment rules and study compatibility.
6. Revision/provenance: source revision, approval, validity, stale dependencies and migration lineage.
7. Operational/security authorization: actor, policy and permitted action, separate from data validity.

Validation results are typed and machine-readable, with code, severity, object/field path, violated rule, expected/actual context, source revision, remediation guidance and whether the finding blocks a particular operation. A project can be structurally loadable but not engineering-valid; a value can be semantically valid but stale; a result can be valid for an old revision but not current; a user can be authorized to inspect but not modify its source.

### U. Data lineage, selective invalidation and reproducibility

Derived data declares dependencies at the smallest meaningful semantic granularity. A change to one CT calibration or one relay element setting should invalidate dependent values/decisions, not every project calculation. Dependency records identify source object/field/revision, transformation/model version, output, evaluation time and dependency scope.

A result binds to an immutable input snapshot and relevant schema/model/solver versions. Reproducibility requires canonical values, units, bases, time context, assumptions, environment/backend details and transformation provenance. A result is not reproducible merely because the project file is available.

Schema migration can itself change interpretation and therefore creates a provenance activity and new revision. Historical outputs remain bound to the schema/model under which they were created. Re-evaluation under a new schema or solver creates a new result, not an overwrite of historical evidence.

### V. UI/UX requirements for engineering data

The Inspector and data editors should show engineering value, unit, quantity kind, source/status, uncertainty/quality, reference conditions, effective date, revision and validation state in context. Avoid presenting a bare number without unit and source. Distinguish source value from converted/display value and show conversion details when relevant.

Editors provide dimension-aware unit selection, valid range and domain-specific constraints, explicit phase/basis/reference context, and clear handling of unknown/not-applicable values. Pasting/importing a value with incompatible unit is rejected or staged for explicit conversion; never silently strip unit suffixes.

Schema/version warnings identify affected objects, migration path, unsupported extensions and possible data loss. Users can inspect field definition, source and lineage without navigating arbitrary JSON. Advanced users may access structured payload views, but raw JSON is not the primary engineering UX.

### W. Candidate acceptance and usability scenarios

1. **UI-ACC-DATA-01** — Renaming an equipment tag does not change stable entity ID or break references.
2. **UI-ACC-DATA-02** — A project retains multiple structured IEC 81346 reference-designation aspects without conflating them with identity.
3. **UI-ACC-DATA-03** — A quantity editor rejects incompatible dimensions and preserves source unit, converted value and conversion provenance.
4. **UI-ACC-DATA-04** — Absolute temperature and temperature difference use distinct semantics and correct conversion.
5. **UI-ACC-DATA-05** — A per-unit value without explicit applicable base context is rejected for study calculation.
6. **UI-ACC-DATA-06** — A voltage/phasor value records RMS/peak convention, phase reference, frequency, phase set and quality where applicable.
7. **UI-ACC-DATA-07** — Unknown, absent, not applicable, invalid and intentionally cleared values remain distinguishable through save/load/export.
8. **UI-ACC-DATA-08** — Manufacturer, nameplate, field-measured, calculated and estimated values retain distinct provenance and conflict-resolution history.
9. **UI-ACC-DATA-09** — A schema registry shows owner, version, status, dependencies, effective date and migration policy.
10. **UI-ACC-DATA-10** — A breaking semantic schema change receives a major version and cannot silently reinterpret existing project data.
11. **UI-ACC-DATA-11** — A lossless migration preserves IDs, units, provenance, extension payloads and relationships.
12. **UI-ACC-DATA-12** — A migration requiring engineering assumptions pauses for explicit review and records the chosen decision.
13. **UI-ACC-DATA-13** — Downgrade/export reports unsupported fields, semantics, precision and evidence rather than claiming full equivalence.
14. **UI-ACC-DATA-14** — Unknown extension fields survive a read-only round trip or are explicitly quarantined; they are never silently dropped.
15. **UI-ACC-DATA-15** — A plugin extension cannot shadow or override a canonical Core field or quantity definition.
16. **UI-ACC-DATA-16** — A derived study result exposes input snapshot, schema versions, units/bases, solver/model version and provenance lineage.
17. **UI-ACC-DATA-17** — Changing one source field identifies affected derived descendants without invalidating unrelated results.
18. **UI-ACC-DATA-18** — Valid time and recorded time can be queried independently for historical engineering facts where bitemporal semantics apply.
19. **UI-ACC-DATA-19** — A reference link to the wrong object type, missing entity or different project is reported precisely.
20. **UI-ACC-DATA-20** — A schema or standard edition mapping records exact source/target versions and known mapping loss.
21. **UI-ACC-DATA-21** — A CIM/SCL/STEP import stages mappings and diagnostics before mutating canonical project state.
22. **UI-ACC-DATA-22** — Canonical serialization produces deterministic content under a declared canonicalization version without using content hash as entity identity.
23. **UI-ACC-DATA-23** — A localized UI label change does not alter persisted enum codes or canonical engineering meaning.
24. **UI-ACC-DATA-24** — Historical reports and calculations remain interpretable under original schema/model versions after a later migration.

### X. Open decisions, dependencies and gates

Open decisions include stable ID format/namespace scope; identity merge/import collision policy; designation-aspect model; schema registry ownership/governance; schema language and validation runtime; canonical quantity storage policy; unit code system/licensed dictionary strategy; quantity-kind ontology and dimension vectors; affine/logarithmic/per-unit semantics; decimal/floating/complex numeric policy by domain; precision/tolerance policy; phase/reference-frame conventions; null/unknown/not-applicable semantics; provenance graph storage/query model; bitemporal scope; event/command/API versioning; schema compatibility matrix; unknown-field preservation; migration signing/rollback; extension namespace governance; canonical JSON normalization/hash profile; CIM/SCL/STEP exchange profiles; standards licensing; BIS adoption and Indian terminology; validation severity/blocking rules; and historical result reproducibility guarantees.

Dependencies: 8I-12 cross-domain traceability; 8I-20 Inspector/property editing; 8I-21 diagnostics/events; 8I-22 collaboration/change control; 8I-23 persistence/recovery; 8I-24 exchange/interoperability; 8I-25 standards traceability; 8I-26 solver governance; 8I-28 through 8I-32 equipment/network/model/calibration architecture; 8I-33 signal/measurement infrastructure; 8I-34 Protection/Control signal consumers; 8I-35 operational lifecycle; 8I-36 event/alarm/SOE/historian/audit; 8I-37 reporting/evidence; 8I-38 asset lifecycle; and 8I-39 cybersecurity/functional safety.

UI-GATE-02 Project/session, UI-GATE-03 Diagnostics, UI-GATE-04 Accessibility/platform, UI-GATE-05 Display/performance, UI-GATE-06 Cross-domain trace and UI-GATE-07 Scope/priority remain open. This entry closes no gate. Data ownership, schema governance, units, compatibility, migration, standards mappings and reproducibility require review by Core/domain architects, electrical engineers, metrology/measurement specialists, numerical solver owners, plugin maintainers, data-exchange specialists and project governance before approval.

### Y. Frozen invariants and research boundary

- Domain-owned canonical schemas remain authoritative; there is no universal untyped engineering property bag.
- Stable entity identity is distinct from tag, name, reference designation, serial number and external system key.
- Engineering quantities require explicit semantic kind, dimension, unit and applicable basis/reference context.
- Electrical phase, sequence, RMS/peak, sign, vector group, reference frame and per-unit bases are explicit where relevant.
- Source value, converted value, display value, calculated value and estimated value are distinct.
- Provenance and lineage are revision-aware; historical results are immutable and reproducible against original inputs/contracts.
- Schema version, project package version, API version, event version, plugin contract version and external standards edition are separate.
- Published schemas are immutable; incompatible semantic changes require explicit versioning and migration.
- Migrations do not invent engineering values or silently discard unknown data.
- Downgrade is potentially lossy and must disclose loss.
- Canonical serialization and content hashing do not replace stable entity identity.
- External standards/dictionaries inform mappings but do not automatically replace GridForge canonical domain models.
- JSON Schema provides structural validation, not complete engineering semantic validation.
- Core/Application/UI/plugin ownership boundaries remain frozen.
- The .gridforge package root remains manifest.json plus canonical project.json; this section does not authorize a competing persistence root.
- V2 main remains unchanged. V3 proposals require review and approval before implementation.

**Scope boundary:** research register only. No schema registry, canonical data model implementation, unit engine, dimensional-analysis runtime, migration framework, provenance database, semantic versioning service, CIM/SCL/STEP adapter, validator, UI, source code, runtime behavior, benchmark, test or CI was implemented or executed. Targeted official-source checks were performed for selected publications and specifications; no complete BIS catalogue verification, standards licensing review, conformance assessment or project-wide schema inventory was completed. V2 main remains unchanged.


## 8I-41. Proposed V3 engineering assurance, configuration baselines, verification, validation and controlled release architecture (2026-11-04)

### 8I-41.1. Research scope and assurance objective

This section defines a traceable engineering assurance lifecycle from requirements and design through analysis, review, factory/site testing, commissioning, acceptance, operational release and as-operated configuration. It is a V3 research proposal, not an assertion of current implementation or standards conformity.

The architecture must distinguish:
- Verification: objective evidence that a work product satisfies specified requirements.
- Validation: evidence that the resulting system satisfies intended use and stakeholder needs in its operational context.
- Review: a defined examination by competent reviewers; review alone is not verification or acceptance.
- Acceptance: an authorized stakeholder's formal disposition of a defined deliverable/scope and its deviations.
- Operational release: authorization to use a particular approved configuration for a stated operational purpose and boundary.
- Commissioning: controlled activities demonstrating installation, integration and functional readiness against project-specific procedures.
- Handover: transfer of defined configuration, records, responsibilities and outstanding actions; not an implicit acceptance of unresolved safety-critical deviations.

No single status field may represent all of these concepts.

### 8I-41.2. Assurance object model

Propose distinct, revision-bound objects:
- Requirement, stakeholder need, design constraint, regulatory/contractual obligation and acceptance criterion.
- System breakdown structure, engineering scope, subsystem, equipment, functional location and interface.
- Configuration item and configuration baseline.
- Design artifact, model, calculation, study case, drawing, schedule, specification and report.
- Verification/validation plan, procedure, test case, test run, observation, measurement, evidence item and result.
- Review record, finding, nonconformance, deviation, concession, waiver, corrective action and closure evidence.
- FAT/FIT/SAT/SIT package, inspection/test certificate, loop-check record, commissioning package and performance-test record.
- Acceptance certificate, release authorization, handover package and as-operated baseline.

These are related by typed references and evidence links, not by copying mutable status text between records. A test run must identify the exact subject revision, procedure revision, test environment, equipment/instrument identity and calibration state, operator, witness where applicable, timestamps, raw observations, acceptance criteria and disposition.

### 8I-41.3. Requirements and traceability

Requirements need stable identity, source, authority, rationale, owner, applicability, priority, verification method, validation method, acceptance criteria, revision, status and approval provenance.

Support bidirectional traceability:
- stakeholder need → system requirement → subsystem/equipment requirement → design element;
- requirement → implementation/model/configuration item;
- requirement → verification method and test case;
- test case → execution, observations and evidence;
- finding/deviation → corrective action → retest or approved disposition;
- requirement → accepted baseline and release decision.

Traceability completeness must be measurable. A link is not proof of satisfaction. A requirement marked verified must point to valid evidence and an approved disposition. Unverified, not-applicable, deferred, waived and rejected states must remain distinct and carry rationale/authority.

### 8I-41.4. Verification and validation separation

Verification is work-product and requirement oriented. Validation is context-of-use and intended-outcome oriented. The system must support analytical verification, inspection, demonstration, simulation, test, independent calculation and review as distinct methods with defined applicability.

A successful power-flow convergence, relay logic simulation, Control sequence simulation, model check or report generation is not automatically proof that the complete plant is safe, correctly installed or fit for service.

Verification evidence must record:
- subject revision and dependency snapshot;
- requirement and acceptance criterion revisions;
- method, procedure, tool and tool version;
- input dataset, model fidelity, assumptions and operating conditions;
- expected and observed outcomes, tolerances and uncertainty;
- execution environment and relevant hardware/software configuration;
- reviewer/witness, approval and timestamp;
- anomalies, deviations, limitations and reproducibility status.

Validation records additionally describe the user/operational context, representative scenarios, boundaries, stakeholder participation, limitations and residual risks.

### 8I-41.5. Engineering configuration identification and baselines

Adopt configuration-management concepts consistent with ISO 10007 as a candidate reference:
- configuration management plan and authority;
- configuration item identification and unique identity;
- baseline definition and controlled change;
- configuration status accounting;
- configuration audit and evidence retention.

A baseline is an immutable, named, revisioned set of identified configuration items and their dependency relationships. It must include exact references to electrical topology, equipment data, SLD layout, instrument/measurement configuration, Protection settings, Control logic, study inputs, model/library versions, solver/tool versions and relevant external interface definitions.

Baseline types are distinct: requirements baseline, design baseline, approved-for-procurement baseline, approved-for-construction baseline, FAT baseline, installed/as-built baseline, commissioned baseline, accepted baseline and as-operated baseline. A project may use a subset or project-specific names, but transitions and scope must be explicit.

A baseline is not merely a Git branch, commit, file timestamp or latest saved project. Git provenance may support source change traceability but cannot replace engineering configuration identity and approval.

### 8I-41.6. Change control and impact assessment

Every proposed change creates a change record with origin, reason, initiator, affected scope, requested effective date, risk class and disposition. Change impact is computed across explicit dependency and relationship graphs: topology, equipment, instrument channels, Protection elements, Control logic, studies, reports, interfaces, commissioning evidence and released baselines.

Impact analysis must distinguish:
- technically affected artifacts;
- potentially affected artifacts requiring review;
- evidence invalidated by changed assumptions or dependencies;
- evidence that remains valid because its immutable inputs and scope are unchanged;
- external approvals and site procedures requiring reauthorization.

Never invalidate all evidence merely because a project revision number changed. Conversely, never retain a verified/accepted status when a relevant dependency changed. Selective invalidation must use dependency identity and revision, not tag/name similarity alone.

A change to a released baseline produces a new candidate baseline. It must not mutate the accepted historical baseline or rewrite prior test evidence. Emergency changes require a defined expedited path, compensating review, traceability and subsequent reconciliation; emergency does not mean undocumented.

### 8I-41.7. Independent review and separation of duties

Support configurable review policies based on risk and project governance:
- author, checker, approver, witness, acceptance authority and release authority are distinct roles;
- self-approval is prohibited where policy requires independent review;
- two-person control applies to selected high-consequence changes;
- review scope and competence requirements are explicit;
- comments, findings, responses, closure evidence and dissent are retained.

The system must not assume every project needs identical approval chains. Policy profiles are configurable, but authority and separation-of-duty constraints cannot be bypassed by UI, plugin or report template.

### 8I-41.8. Test architecture and test evidence

Model test definition separately from execution. A reusable test case contains preconditions, configuration, steps, stimulus, expected result, tolerance, safety constraints, required instruments, evidence capture and pass/fail/blocked/inconclusive rules.

A test run is immutable evidence. Re-running a test creates a new run; it does not overwrite a failed or superseded run. Support manual, instrument-assisted, automated, simulated and hybrid execution with explicit method and confidence boundaries.

Test results must include raw observations where practicable, normalized engineering quantities, unit/reference conditions, timestamps and time quality, instrument calibration, measurement uncertainty, environment, operator and witnesses. A pass result cannot be generated from missing mandatory evidence. Tolerance comparison must account for units, precision, rounding, uncertainty and acceptance-rule version.

Simulation evidence must identify simulator/model/solver versions, model fidelity, assumptions, initial conditions, input snapshots, time step or solver settings and hardware execution path where relevant. Simulation must not be represented as physical FAT/SAT evidence unless the approved procedure explicitly defines the simulated scope.

### 8I-41.9. FAT, FIT, SAT and SIT

Support project-configurable test stages:
- FAT: vendor/factory verification against agreed specification and factory configuration.
- FIT: integration of factory systems or packages before site deployment, where required.
- SAT: verification at the installation site against site conditions and agreed scope.
- SIT: end-to-end integration across systems and interfaces in the site context.

These stages are not universally interchangeable, nor does one passing stage imply all others passed. Each package records boundaries, exclusions, responsibility matrix, configuration under test, witness/hold points, punch items, deviations, retest requirements and signed disposition.

IEC 62381:2024 is the candidate reference for automation-system FAT/FIT/SAT/SIT planning. GridForge should provide configurable evidence structures, not hard-code one industry or contract's checklist as universal.

### 8I-41.10. Electrical, instrumentation, Protection and Control commissioning

Commissioning procedures must be domain-specific while sharing evidence infrastructure:
- Electrical: installation inspection, continuity, insulation, earthing, phasing, transformer and switchgear tests, CT/PT polarity/ratio and relevant functional tests.
- Instrumentation: instrument identity, range, calibration, loop checks, wiring, channel mapping, scaling, quality and end-to-end signal verification.
- Protection: CT/PT measurement path, relay settings revision, element enablement, injection test evidence, trip matrix, breaker interface, trip circuit supervision and approved functional test results.
- Control: I/O checks, interlock/permissive logic, sequence tests, fail-state behavior, communication loss response, alarm and operator-interface verification.
- Integrated systems: trip/interlock cause-and-effect, command/feedback reconciliation, time synchronization, event sequence and interface behavior.

Protection testing evidence must not be confused with authorization to operate or proof of actual fault-clearing performance in every possible network condition. Control simulation must not be represented as validation of physical actuator behavior unless the physical interface has been tested.

GridForge remains an engineering evidence and workflow platform; it does not replace site permit-to-work, isolation/LOTO, switching authorization, safety management or owner-approved commissioning authority.

### 8I-41.11. Nonconformance, punch lists and deviations

Findings need severity, safety/operational consequence, affected configuration, discovery stage, owner, due date, containment, root-cause status, corrective action and closure criteria.

Disposition options include correction, retest, accepted deviation/concession, deferred action with restrictions, rejection or no-fault-found. Waivers and concessions require named authority, rationale, scope, expiry/review condition and compensating controls. A waiver does not silently rewrite the original requirement or turn a failed test into a pass.

Punch-list items must carry stage, priority, responsibility, due date, blocking status and evidence of closure. Safety-critical and Protection/Control functional defects must be blocked from release according to project policy; a generic severity label must not override defined release constraints.

### 8I-41.12. Acceptance, handover and release gates

Acceptance is a decision over a named scope and baseline. The acceptance package identifies deliverables, evidence index, deviations, outstanding punch items, residual risks, exclusions, warranties/interfaces and authorized signatories.

Release states should be explicit and policy-configurable, for example:
- draft / under development;
- submitted for review;
- verified;
- validated for stated use;
- approved for procurement/construction;
- approved for factory/site testing;
- commissioned;
- accepted with stated conditions;
- released for defined operation;
- superseded / withdrawn / suspended.

These are not necessarily a single linear enum. A design can be verified while not validated; a system can be commissioned with open non-blocking punch items; an accepted baseline can later be superseded without losing historical acceptance. State transitions require guards, evidence, actor authority and audit events.

Operational release must be tied to the exact installed/commissioned baseline, approved operating boundary, restrictions, protection/control configuration and outstanding conditions. It must not automatically actuate equipment or issue commands to plant systems.

### 8I-41.13. As-built and as-operated reconciliation

Maintain distinct as-designed, as-procured, as-manufactured, as-installed, as-tested, as-commissioned, as-accepted and as-operated records. A difference is a typed deviation/change, not a silent overwrite.

Support redline capture, field markups, actual tag/serial/terminal mapping, equipment replacement, instrument calibration state, firmware/settings versions and field-measured parameters. Reconciliation must identify whether the change is documentation-only, engineering-affecting, safety-affecting, Protection/Control-affecting or requires new verification/commissioning.

The as-operated baseline is a controlled snapshot of known configuration and effective time, not a claim that every live device has been continuously observed. Device readback and communication evidence must carry source, timestamp, quality and completeness.

### 8I-41.14. Evidence integrity and reproducibility

Reuse 8I-36 event/audit/historian architecture and 8I-37 report provenance. Evidence objects are immutable after finalization; corrections are appended as amendments with actor, reason and links to the superseded item.

Integrity hashes establish content identity, not signer identity or engineering validity. Where signatures are used, record signer identity, certificate chain/trust policy, signing time, revocation/validation evidence and the exact signed payload. Preserve original raw data, derived values, calculation method and transformation lineage.

Long-term evidence packages must remain interpretable when plugins, tools, libraries or certificates become unavailable. Store schema and format identifiers, relevant metadata, versioned procedures and durable export options. Do not promise perpetual executable reproducibility when external runtimes or hardware are no longer available; distinguish reproducible inputs, reproducible method and reproducible execution.

### 8I-41.15. Cross-domain evidence integration

Assurance records must link to:
- Core domain objects and physical topology;
- Application commands, approvals and change transactions;
- Signal and Measurement Infrastructure samples, quality and calibration;
- Protection decisions, settings and test results;
- Control logic revisions, scan/task configuration and interlock evidence;
- study snapshots, solver versions, assumptions and results;
- asset lifecycle, maintenance and inspection records;
- operational command/feedback/SOE and historian evidence;
- report packages, external exchange and cybersecurity audit records.

A shared evidence graph provides navigation and traceability, but domain owners retain authority over technical meaning and acceptance rules. No generic assurance engine may reinterpret a Protection trip, Control interlock or electrical validation result.

### 8I-41.16. Data model and event contracts

Candidate canonical records include RequirementRevision, ConfigurationItemRevision, BaselineManifest, VerificationPlan, ValidationPlan, TestProcedureRevision, TestExecution, EvidenceRecord, Finding, Deviation, ReviewDecision, AcceptanceDecision, ReleaseAuthorization and HandoverPackage.

Every record needs stable identity, immutable revision, typed status, effective time, recorded time, provenance, actor/authority, scope and links to source revisions. Events include RequirementChanged, BaselineProposed, BaselineApproved, TestStarted, TestCompleted, EvidenceFinalized, FindingRaised, DeviationAuthorized, AcceptanceGranted, ReleaseAuthorized and BaselineSuperseded.

Events are evidence of recorded actions, not substitutes for authoritative current state or transactional command validation.

### 8I-41.17. UI/UX and role workflows

Provide an assurance workspace with:
- requirement-to-evidence trace matrix and gap indicators;
- baseline comparison and impact review;
- verification/validation plan and execution views;
- FAT/FIT/SAT/SIT and commissioning dashboards;
- findings, punch list and deviation disposition;
- review/approval queues with authority context;
- acceptance and release dossier builder;
- as-built/as-operated reconciliation.

Show why an item is blocked, what evidence is missing, which dependency invalidated it and who can authorize the next transition. Distinguish pass, fail, blocked, inconclusive, not applicable, waived and not yet executed with text and icon/shape cues, not colour alone. Never display a green compliance/acceptance indicator merely because all checklist boxes were clicked.

### 8I-41.18. Security, safety and authority constraints

Apply 8I-39 identity, authorization, signature and audit requirements to every approval and release. Approval must bind to exact payload hashes and revisions. A change after approval invalidates the approval for the changed scope.

Functional safety and electrical Protection requirements remain independently governed. GridForge assurance status cannot certify a safety instrumented function, relay, switchgear, installation or plant unless the applicable competent authority and certification process have done so. No plugin, report generator or administrator override may fabricate test evidence, bypass Core invariants or issue unauthorized operational commands.

### 8I-41.19. Candidate standards and applicability map

Candidate references for later clause-level verification:
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 — system lifecycle processes.
- ISO 10007:2017 — configuration management guidance; revision status requires monitoring.
- IEC 62381:2024 — automation FAT/FIT/SAT/SIT.
- IEC 62337:2012 — electrical, instrumentation and control commissioning phases/milestones.
- IEC 61508 and IEC 61511 — functional safety lifecycle where applicable; verify current editions, amendments and national adoption before use.
- ISO 9001 — quality management system context, where applicable.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289 — lifecycle information item content, candidate for documentation governance.
- ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 — requirements engineering, candidate for requirement quality and traceability.

This is a candidate map, not verified BIS adoption, clause-by-clause compliance, certification or a legal applicability determination. Project-specific contracts, owner specifications, statutory rules and jurisdictional requirements take precedence where applicable.

### 8I-41.20. Proposed acceptance scenarios

Candidate scenarios for later V3 acceptance planning:
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-01: Trace a stakeholder need through approved requirements, design, test and release evidence.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-02: Prevent verification status without a valid requirement-linked evidence record.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-03: Distinguish verification from validation in the user workflow.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-04: Preserve immutable failed test execution when a retest passes.
