- UI-ACC-ASSURE-05: Bind a test run to exact procedure, subject and dependency revisions.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-06: Reject a test pass when mandatory observations or calibration evidence are missing.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-07: Record measurement uncertainty and apply versioned acceptance tolerances.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-08: Separate simulated evidence from physical FAT/SAT evidence.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-09: Create and compare immutable design, construction and as-built baselines.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-10: Invalidate only evidence affected by a relevant dependency change.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-11: Preserve evidence whose immutable inputs and scope remain unchanged.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-12: Require independent review for policy-designated high-consequence changes.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-13: Prevent unauthorized self-approval or separation-of-duty bypass.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-14: Manage FAT, FIT, SAT and SIT as distinct scoped stages.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-15: Capture electrical, instrumentation, Protection and Control commissioning evidence independently.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-16: Prevent a Protection settings test pass from implying plant operational authorization.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-17: Record nonconformance, corrective action, retest and closure lineage.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-18: Require authorized, scoped and expiring concession for accepted deviations.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-19: Block release when mandatory safety-critical findings remain unresolved.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-20: Grant acceptance only for a named baseline and defined scope.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-21: Preserve historical acceptance after a newer baseline supersedes it.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-22: Bind operational release to exact commissioned configuration and restrictions.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-23: Reconcile field redlines and device readback without silently overwriting design intent.
- UI-ACC-ASSURE-24: Export a durable handover dossier with provenance, signatures and evidence index.

### 8I-41.21. Open architectural decisions

1. Define the minimum universal assurance object model versus project-configurable profiles.
2. Decide whether requirements authoring is native V3 capability or integrated through external requirements-management systems.
3. Define baseline granularity and the canonical manifest format across engineering domains.
4. Define approval/signature trust policy, certificate lifecycle and offline signing behavior.
5. Define policy profiles for FAT/FIT/SAT/SIT, commissioning, acceptance and release.
6. Define how field/device readback is reconciled with the as-operated baseline when connectivity is partial or data quality is poor.
7. Define long-term evidence retention, export formats and archival validation.
8. Define risk-class thresholds and non-waivable release constraints without hard-coding one owner's governance model.
9. Verify applicable BIS adoptions, editions, amendments and contract-specific requirements before any compliance claims.

### 8I-41.22. UI/UX gate impact

This section adds evidence and review needs to UI-GATE-02 (project/session lifecycle), UI-GATE-03 (diagnostics and evidence), UI-GATE-06 (cross-domain traceability) and UI-GATE-07 (scope and priority). UI-GATE-04 and UI-GATE-05 remain relevant to accessible assurance dashboards and large evidence sets. All gates remain open pending explicit decisions and acceptance evidence.

### 8I-41.23. Frozen V2 invariants and V3 migration boundary

Preserve the frozen V2 architecture as the baseline: Core owns domain truth; Application owns commands, services and controlled mutation; UI remains projection and interaction; plugins use public contracts and Application services; Protection and Control remain separate execution authorities; project persistence remains the canonical engineering project package.

V3 assurance capabilities must not introduce Qt/UI dependencies into Core, permit plugin bypass of Application, conflate project revisions with engineering baselines, or turn report/test evidence into mutable status flags. Migration is additive and requires explicit approval; this research does not authorize V2 source changes.

### 8I-41.24. Research disposition

Research-only proposal. No implementation, tests, CI, benchmarks, runtime validation, certification or compliance assessment was performed. No changes to V2 main. UI-GATE-02 through UI-GATE-07 remain open. BIS catalogue verification for Protection, Automation and Control remains a separate outstanding evidence task.


## 8I-42. Proposed V3 multidisciplinary plant engineering and physical-system integration architecture (2026-11-04)

### 8I-42.1. Scope and architectural objective

Coordinate electrical, mechanical, process, instrumentation, control, civil, structural and spatial engineering without collapsing them into one geometry-centric model. The objective is consistent multidisciplinary engineering and change-impact traceability, not a universal plant object.

Maintain independently governed but linked representations:
- electrical network topology, terminals, connectivity and study abstractions;
- physical assets, installation positions, spatial envelopes and maintenance access;
- instrumentation devices, loops, channels, signal paths and calibration;
- cables, conductors, trays, ducts, conduits and routing systems;
- mechanical equipment, shafts, couplings, loads and package interfaces;
- process equipment, piping systems, line lists, nozzles and process connections;
- civil/structural models, foundations, supports, platforms, buildings and penetrations;
- 2D drawings, 3D coordination models, BIM/CAD references and field markups.

A common asset identity does not imply a common domain model. A geometry clash must not mutate electrical connectivity; an electrical connection must not imply a physically routed or installed cable; a detailed 3D object must not become the source of engineering calculations merely because it is visually rich.

### 8I-42.2. Plant breakdown, locations and identity

Model plant hierarchy separately from spatial containment and functional relationships. Candidate hierarchy: site, plant, area, unit, system, subsystem, package, equipment and component. Functional location, physical installation position, electrical network location, process location, building/room/level/grid and asset identity are distinct typed references.

Stable equipment/asset identity must survive tag changes, relocation, replacement in a functional location, movement between projects, and changes to drawing numbers or external BIM identifiers. External IDs and discipline tags are aliases with source-system provenance, not universal primary keys. A functional location may persist across equipment replacement; a physical equipment instance may move. Preserve temporal history and effective dates.

### 8I-42.3. Discipline ownership and authority boundaries

Define ownership by technical meaning, not file format:
- Electrical Core owns electrical equipment semantics, terminals, connectivity, topology and electrical validation.
- Mechanical/process models own their equipment, interfaces and discipline calculations when introduced.
- Instrumentation and Signal infrastructure owns instrument identity, channels, measurement semantics, signal routing, quality and calibration.
- Protection and Control remain separate execution authorities.
- Civil/structural models own foundations, structural members, loads and constraints when supported.
- Spatial coordination owns reference frames, placement, envelopes, clearances and clash findings, not the engineering truth of connected systems.
- Application owns cross-domain commands, transactions, orchestration, controlled mutation and revision coordination.
- UI presents coordinated projections and discipline-specific editing experiences.
- Plugins contribute through public contracts and Application services; no plugin may mutate Core directly.

Do not create a monolithic PlantObject with every discipline field optional. Use bounded contexts and typed cross-domain references.

### 8I-42.4. Coordinate reference and spatial semantics

Spatial data must declare coordinate reference system, units, axis orientation, origin, handedness, elevation datum, local/project/site transform, precision and transformation provenance. Distinguish geodetic, site/project, building/area, equipment-local, drawing/sheet and model-local coordinates.

Every transform must be explicit and versioned. Avoid implicit assumptions about millimetres/metres, Z-up/Y-up, north direction, elevation datum or handedness. Preserve transformation chains and source model metadata.

Geometry must identify its representation and purpose: symbolic footprint, bounding box, simplified envelope, detailed solid, mesh, centreline, route path, point cloud or 2D annotation. A bounding box is not a certified clearance envelope. A display mesh is not a fabrication model. Precision and tolerances must be declared, not inferred from pixels.

### 8I-42.5. Equipment spatial representation and maintainability

Equipment placement references stable asset/equipment identity and retains insertion point, orientation, coordinate frame, placement revision, envelope type/source, service/operation/removal/maintenance clearances, access zones, lifting/removal path, transport envelope, nozzle/terminal/cable-entry/shaft/foundation interfaces, weight, centre of gravity, support loads, provenance and installation state.

Clearance checks distinguish mandatory code/owner constraints, manufacturer recommendations, project rules and heuristic warnings. A clash result includes rule/source, geometry revisions, tolerance, severity, uncertainty and disposition. Never label a heuristic overlap a code violation without an applicable verified rule.

### 8I-42.6. Electrical topology versus physical connectivity

The electrical network graph remains authoritative for electrical connectivity. Spatial models may display equipment location, terminals, cable routes and physical interfaces, but geometry touching must not create or delete electrical edges.

Distinguish electrical terminal connection, physical conductor/cable assembly, cable cores and terminations, tray/duct/conduit route, containment/support, wiring-diagram representation and as-installed connection evidence. A physical cable route is not itself electrical topology; an abstract electrical connection may exist before routing is designed. Preserve traceability from terminal to cable/core/termination and installation evidence.

Busbars, overhead lines, underground cables, bus ducts, GIS conductors and internal equipment connections need domain-appropriate physical representations. Do not force every electrical connection into a generic cable segment.

### 8I-42.7. Cable, tray and routing architecture

Model cable as a typed physical assembly with stable identity, service, voltage class, conductor/core structure, material, insulation, screen/armour, length, terminations, route and status. Keep cable schedule, electrical model parameters and physical routing linked but distinct.

Routing networks include tray, ladder, trench, duct, conduit, tunnel, riser, building penetration and direct-buried segments. Routes may need segment geometry, containment capacity, fill/occupancy, bend radius, separation, fire barriers, environment, support spacing and accessibility.

A shortest path is not automatically acceptable. Consider electrical segregation, EMC, fire zones, hazardous areas, heat derating, maintainability, installation sequence and spare capacity. Preliminary cable length is an estimate, not an approved construction quantity.

### 8I-42.8. Instrumentation and signal physical integration

Link field instrument identity to physical location, process connection, instrument loop, signal channel, cable/core, marshalling cabinet, I/O card/channel and consuming Control/Protection function as distinct relationships.

Instrument location, tapping point, impulse tubing, thermowell, sample line, junction box and cable route are not substitutes for measurement semantics. The shared Signal and Measurement Infrastructure from 8I-33 remains authoritative for typed values, units, quality, timestamp, calibration and processing. Spatial routing adds installation/accessibility evidence, not measurement validity.

A physical wiring or channel assignment change triggers impact assessment for affected consumers and Protection/Control elements without indiscriminately invalidating unrelated electrical topology.

### 8I-42.9. Mechanical and process interfaces

Use typed interface contracts for supported mechanical/process scope: shaft/coupling, nozzle, flange, piping tie-in, support, load, rotation direction, speed, torque, fluid/service, pressure, temperature, vibration and package boundary. These are not generic untyped ports.

Mechanical trains and process flow paths are separate graphs from electrical topology. A motor may connect electrically to a bus and mechanically to a driven load; those relationships remain independently traceable. Pump nozzles do not become electrical terminals. Detailed piping stress, fluid dynamics or structural analysis must not be claimed until the corresponding domain solver and validation scope are designed.

### 8I-42.10. Civil, structural and building coordination

Support references to foundations, plinths, anchor bolts, embedded plates, structural steel, supports, trenches, buildings, rooms, platforms, access ways and penetrations. Physical loads and reactions require source, units, load case, combination and approval provenance.

Spatial coordination may identify conflicts among equipment, foundation, steelwork, tray, piping, access route or building opening. Structural adequacy requires discipline-specific calculation and authorized review; clash-free geometry is not proof of structural safety. Geometry-only changes must not silently alter accepted load assumptions or certified calculations.

### 8I-42.11. 2D drawings, 3D models and BIM/CAD interoperability

Treat drawings and federated models as controlled representations with source identity, revision, coordinate reference, discipline, scope, authoring application/version, exchange settings and fidelity metadata.

Potential exchange families:
- IFC for building/infrastructure BIM exchange, subject to supported schema/view and implementation validation;
- ISO 10303 STEP for product/engineering geometry and product data;
- DXF/DWG and other CAD formats, subject to licensing and implementation constraints;
- BCF for issue/clash communication where supported;
- discipline-native formats such as electrical SLD/SCL and plant design formats through explicit adapters.

No format becomes the canonical GridForge domain model by default. Import adapters stage, validate, map and report loss before controlled acceptance. Export adapters operate on immutable revision-bound snapshots. Preserve identity, units, coordinate transforms, provenance, topology references and unsupported extension data where feasible. Assign explicit fidelity grades and document dropped, approximated or flattened information.

### 8I-42.12. Model federation and clash detection

Federation composes read-only or controlled references from discipline models. Each source retains its revision and authority. A federation manifest records model identity, revision, coordinate transform, discipline, scope, units, visibility and load status.

Differentiate hard geometric interference, clearance/access violation, maintenance/removal envelope conflict, route capacity/segregation conflict, structural support/foundation conflict, interface mismatch, data/identity inconsistency and schedule/sequence conflict.

A clash is a reviewable issue, not an automatic design mutation. Record source object references and revisions, rule, geometric method, tolerance, severity, responsible discipline, status, resolution proposal, approval and retest. Accepted exceptions require explicit scope and expiry/review conditions.

### 8I-42.13. Revision, change impact and synchronization

Discipline models evolve at different rates. Federation records each source revision and detects stale references. Synchronization is controlled exchange, not silent overwrite or bidirectional last-write-wins merge.

Impact analysis identifies affected electrical equipment/topology, instrument channels, Protection/Control dependencies, cable schedules/routes, mechanical/process interfaces, structural calculations, drawings, asset baselines, studies, reports and commissioning evidence.

A geometry-only move may leave connectivity unchanged but affect cable length, clearance, access, foundation and installation evidence. A terminal change may affect topology, termination, instrument loop and tests. A tag change may affect references/deliverables without changing physical or electrical behavior. Dependency-specific invalidation preserves unaffected evidence.

### 8I-42.14. Installation, construction and field reconciliation

Support design, approved-for-construction, construction, redline, installed and as-built states as separate baselines. Field capture includes actual location/orientation, tag/serial, terminal/connection, cable route, support, foundation, deviations, photographs/document references and survey source.

Observations carry recorder, time, coordinate system, accuracy, survey method and confidence. Mobile/offline capture preserves provenance and synchronizes through conflict-aware change sets. A field markup is proposed evidence, not automatically an approved design change.

Construction progress is not technical acceptance or operational release. Permit-to-work, isolation, lifting authorization and site safety controls remain external authoritative processes unless a separately approved integration is specified.

### 8I-42.15. Digital twin and operational feedback boundary

A coordinated plant model may combine design geometry, asset metadata, measured signals, alarms/events, maintenance records and device readback. This does not automatically constitute a validated digital twin.

Label data by source and temporal meaning: design intent, model prediction, vendor data, field survey, live measurement, historian record, manual observation and inferred state. Show quality, timestamp, latency and missing coverage. Predicted/inferred geometry must not appear as surveyed fact.

Operational feedback may update a separate observed-state projection and create a proposed engineering change. It must not silently rewrite approved design or as-operated baseline. Reconciliation requires authority, evidence and effective-time semantics.

### 8I-42.16. Performance and rendering architecture

Large models require progressive loading, spatial partitioning, level of detail, view-frustum culling, instancing, geometry simplification, bounded caches and asynchronous preparation. UI rendering remains on the UI thread; heavy geometry processing and federation indexing run in controlled workers/services.

Maintain separate geometry for engineering computation, clash analysis, selection and display. Rendering meshes are disposable projections, never canonical engineering data. Selection resolves to stable domain identity, not transient graphics-item IDs.

Support coordinated 2D/3D navigation, discipline filters, visibility sets, section/clipping planes, saved viewpoints and cross-selection. Accessibility and keyboard navigation remain available; clash status cannot rely only on colour or 3D cues.

### 8I-42.17. Plugin and extension boundaries

Centralize discipline extensions under the governed plugin host. Candidate capabilities include discipline model providers, import/export adapters, geometry readers, clash rule packs, symbol libraries, drawing providers and property editors.

Each plugin declares API/schema compatibility, publisher identity, permissions, data access, file/network/process capabilities and resource limits under 8I-39. Plugin output is untrusted until validated by the owning domain/Application contract. Plugins cannot directly mutate electrical topology, Protection state, Control execution state or accepted baselines.

Avoid separate plugin managers per discipline or duplicated event buses, project persistence, identity, transactions and revision services.

### 8I-42.18. Data governance and canonical records

Candidate records: PlantLocation, FunctionalLocationRef, SpatialPlacement, CoordinateReference, TransformRevision, GeometryRepresentation, InterfaceDefinition, PhysicalRoute, CableAssembly, CableCore, Termination, FoundationReference, FederatedModelManifest, ClashFinding and FieldObservation.

Each carries stable identity, schema revision, source/owner domain, effective/recorded time, units/coordinate reference where relevant, provenance, quality, lifecycle status and links to immutable source revisions. Geometry payloads may be stored separately from project JSON through an explicitly governed package/resource scheme, but the frozen V2 persistence baseline remains unchanged until V3 migration is approved.

Package portability, archive safety, integrity, resource limits and external-reference handling follow the concerns in 8I-23 and 8I-39. Avoid silently embedding huge source models or relying on broken external paths.

### 8I-42.19. Candidate standards and exchange references

Candidate references for later clause-level and edition/adoption verification:
- ISO 19650 series — information management using BIM for buildings and civil engineering works.
- ISO 16739-1 — Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) data schema.
- ISO 10303 series — product data representation and exchange (STEP).
- ISO 12006 series — building construction classification framework.
- ISO 81346 series — structuring principles and reference designations.
- IEC 81346-2 — object classification, subject to current edition/adoption verification.
- IEC 61970/61968 — CIM and utility enterprise integration where applicable.
- IEC 61850-6 — SCL engineering configuration exchange for power utility automation.
- IEC 62424 — process control engineering requests in P&ID tools, where applicable.
- ISO 55000 series — asset management context and lifecycle alignment.
- Relevant national electrical installation, fire, structural, building, hazardous-area and owner standards according to jurisdiction and project scope.

Candidate map only. No clause-level applicability, current edition, BIS adoption, licensing, conformance or certification has been established. Verify official catalogues and project contract/jurisdiction before implementation.

### 8I-42.20. Proposed acceptance scenarios

Candidate scenarios:
- UI-ACC-PLANT-01: Maintain stable equipment identity across electrical, spatial, asset and drawing representations.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-02: Preserve separate functional location and physical asset identity during replacement.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-03: Reject ambiguous coordinate systems or undeclared unit transformations.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-04: Transform federated models while retaining source and transform provenance.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-05: Distinguish equipment envelope, service clearance and removal envelope.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-06: Report a spatial clash without mutating electrical connectivity.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-07: Preserve topology when equipment moves without a topology change.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-08: Require an explicit electrical-domain command for terminal/connectivity changes.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-09: Link terminals to cable cores/terminations without conflating route geometry and topology.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-10: Validate route capacity, bend radius and segregation against versioned rules.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-11: Distinguish preliminary cable length estimate from approved construction quantity.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-12: Trace field instruments through loop, channel, cable and consuming function.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-13: Invalidate affected signal consumers after channel/termination change without invalidating unrelated topology.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-14: Link mechanical shaft/load interfaces to motor assets without treating them as electrical terminals.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-15: Report foundation/equipment conflict without claiming structural adequacy or failure.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-16: Import IFC/STEP/CAD through staging, mapping and fidelity reporting.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-17: Preserve unsupported exchange properties or explicitly report their loss.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-18: Detect stale source revisions in a federated model.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-19: Tie a clash finding to exact source object and geometry revisions.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-20: Resolve and retest a clash while preserving original finding history.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-21: Reconcile field redlines as proposed changes, not silent baseline mutation.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-22: Maintain as-designed, as-installed and as-built representations independently.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-23: Display measured, inferred and predicted plant state with distinct provenance and quality.
- UI-ACC-PLANT-24: Navigate large federated models without making display geometry authoritative.

### 8I-42.21. Open architectural decisions

1. Define V3 discipline scope and sequence: electrical-first coordination, then instrumentation/cabling, followed by mechanical/process and civil/structural references.
2. Decide whether GridForge owns native spatial geometry editing or initially consumes federated read-only references.
3. Select supported coordinate reference systems, transform library and precision policy.
4. Define identity mapping across equipment, assets, functional locations, IFC GUIDs, drawing IDs and vendor package IDs.
5. Decide geometry storage/resource packaging without weakening project portability and archive security.
6. Define initial cable routing and clearance rule scope, source licensing and jurisdiction-specific applicability.
7. Define clash severity, tolerance, issue ownership, waiver and revalidation policies.
8. Define BIM/CAD adapter priorities, supported schemas/views, fidelity grades and licensing constraints.
9. Define which mechanical/process/civil data is authoritative in GridForge versus external systems.
10. Define spatial-model performance budgets and minimum supported workstation hardware.
11. Define field survey and mobile/offline reconciliation contracts.
12. Verify BIS adoptions and project-specific normative requirements before compliance statements.

### 8I-42.22. UI/UX gate impact

Impacts UI-GATE-02 (project/session and model references), UI-GATE-04 (accessibility and multi-view interaction), UI-GATE-05 (large-model rendering performance), UI-GATE-06 (cross-domain identity/traceability) and UI-GATE-07 (scope/priority). UI-GATE-03 remains relevant to clash, import, coordinate and stale-model diagnostics. All gates remain open pending decisions and acceptance evidence.

### 8I-42.23. Frozen V2 invariants and migration boundary

Preserve frozen V2 architecture: Core owns electrical/domain truth; Application owns commands, services and controlled mutation; UI is projection and interaction; plugins use public contracts and Application services; Protection and Control remain separate authorities; the established V2 project package contract remains unchanged.

V3 integration must not introduce geometry or Qt dependencies into electrical Core, make external BIM/CAD models implicit sources of electrical connectivity, permit plugin mutation outside Application or turn rendering objects into persistent domain objects. Package/geometry migration requires explicit V3 approval. This research authorizes no V2 source change.

### 8I-42.24. Research disposition

Research-only proposal. No implementation, tests, CI, benchmarks, runtime validation, standards conformity assessment or certification was performed. V2 main remains unchanged. UI-GATE-02 through UI-GATE-07 remain open. BIS catalogue verification for Protection, Automation and Control remains a separate outstanding task.


## 8I-43. Proposed V3 engineering project execution, work breakdown, deliverable planning, multidisciplinary coordination and engineering progress governance (2026-11-04)

### 8I-43.1. Purpose and product boundary

GridForge V3 should provide engineering-project execution capabilities that connect technical scope, engineering work, deliverables, interfaces, reviews, revisions and readiness evidence. This is not a proposal to recreate a general enterprise project-management suite. The product boundary is engineering information and technical workflow governance: the project execution layer coordinates work whose outputs are engineering objects, calculations, drawings, specifications, models, lists, reports, reviews and controlled technical decisions.

Generic enterprise resource planning (ERP), accounting, contract administration, payroll, procurement transaction processing, contractor timesheets and full construction-management execution remain external system responsibilities unless a separately approved product scope establishes a specific integration. GridForge may exchange controlled references and status with those systems; it must not silently become their system of record.

The execution layer must not own electrical topology, Protection or Control decisions, solver truth, asset condition or commissioning acceptance. Those remain with their respective domain authorities and assurance workflows. Execution records link to those objects and evidence through stable identities and revision-aware references.

### 8I-43.2. Project and execution object model

Candidate hierarchy of concepts:
- EngineeringProject: project identity, scope, contractual context, lifecycle, configuration and governance policy.
- ContractPackage: a contractual or appointment boundary, not a technical system boundary.
- PlantSystem / FunctionalSystem: the plant or technical system being engineered; link to the relevant domain model.
- ScopeItem: an authorized technical or information outcome with inclusion, exclusion, assumptions and acceptance criteria.
- WorkPackage: bounded body of coordinated work with defined inputs, outputs, dependencies, owner, schedule window, effort/resource plan, risks and completion evidence.
- Activity: schedulable work step contributing to a work package; activity completion is not technical acceptance.
- Deliverable: controlled engineering information product with identity, revision, purpose, status, ownership and evidence.
- Milestone: event or decision point with explicit achievement criteria, not an arbitrary date label.
- Interface: managed boundary and exchange obligation between disciplines, packages, suppliers or external systems.
- Review / Comment / Response / Approval / Transmittal: separate workflow and evidence records.
- ChangeRequest / TechnicalQuery / FieldChange / VendorDeviation: typed change-intake records with distinct authority and disposition.
- Decision / Risk / Assumption / Constraint / Issue / Action: linked governance records with ownership and history.

Project identity, technical-system identity, work identity and deliverable identity must not be conflated. One deliverable can support several systems; one system can require many deliverables; one work package can produce multiple deliverables; and one deliverable can depend on multiple upstream interfaces.

### 8I-43.3. Multiple breakdown structures, not one overloaded WBS

Support separate, typed breakdown structures:
1. Project/contract breakdown: project, contract, package, phase and authorized scope.
2. Plant/system breakdown: plant, area, unit, process/electrical system, subsystem and equipment/functional location.
3. Engineering work breakdown: discipline, engineering package, work package and activity.
4. Deliverable breakdown: deliverable class, discipline, system, document/model group and individual information container.
5. Organisational breakdown: organisation, company, team, role and accountable party.
6. Spatial/location breakdown: site, building, level, area, room and physical location where applicable.

These structures may be mapped but must not be collapsed into a single universal tree. A deliverable can be cross-referenced to multiple plant systems and work packages while retaining one canonical identity. Mappings require typed relationship, effective revision, source authority and provenance. WBS changes must not silently renumber or orphan technical assets and deliverables.

A WBS dictionary or equivalent definition should capture scope meaning, inclusion/exclusion, accountable owner, boundary, completion criteria and links to deliverables. Stable machine identifiers must be separate from editable display codes and names. Renumbering must preserve identity and historical references.

### 8I-43.4. Responsibility and authority model

Provide explicit accountable owner, responsible producer, checker, interdisciplinary reviewer, approver, accepting authority and recipient roles. Support RACI-style assignment as a project-configurable governance convention, not as a universal hard-coded workflow. Responsibility assignment is not equivalent to permission: authorization and access control remain governed by the security model in 8I-39.

Segregation-of-duties rules should prevent a person from performing incompatible preparation, independent check and approval roles where the project or safety/quality regime requires separation. Delegation, substitution, temporary assignment and external-party access require scope, validity period and audit history. A role assignment does not confer domain authority to mutate Core or dispatch Protection/Control actions.

### 8I-43.5. Engineering deliverable register and metadata

The deliverable register is a first-class project view. Candidate deliverable classes include:
- Drawings: SLDs, schematics, wiring, layouts, arrangement and interface drawings.
- Engineering calculations and study reports.
- Equipment specifications, datasheets and technical requisitions.
- Equipment, cable, I/O, instrument, terminal, signal and load lists.
- Control narratives, logic diagrams, cause-and-effect matrices and interlock schedules.
- Protection settings, coordination studies and protection philosophies.
- Models, models extracts, federated model packages and exchange datasets.
- Procedures, inspection/test plans, method statements and commissioning documents.
- Technical reports, compliance matrices, design-basis documents and decision records.

Candidate metadata: immutable deliverable ID; project-defined number; title; class; discipline; system/subsystem; scope links; originator; responsible organisation; checker; approver; planned/forecast/actual dates; current revision; lifecycle state; issue purpose; security classification; source references; dependencies; review cycle; acceptance criteria; and evidence links.

A deliverable is a controlled information product, not merely a file. It may have one or more representations/attachments. The canonical record must identify exact content versions and their hashes or equivalent integrity evidence. A file name is not a reliable identity.

### 8I-43.6. Separate workflow, maturity, review and baseline state

Do not compress different meanings into one status field. Maintain distinct axes:
- Production workflow: planned, in preparation, internal check, interdisciplinary review, client/owner review, comment resolution, approved for issue, issued, superseded, withdrawn.
- Technical maturity: concept, preliminary, basic/FEED, detailed, construction-ready, as-built/as-installed, operational handover; configure stages per contract and discipline.
- Review disposition: not reviewed, accepted, accepted with comments, revise/resubmit, rejected, information only, not applicable.
- Issue purpose: for review, information, approval, procurement, construction, commissioning, tender or record; project-configurable.
- Baseline relationship: draft, proposed, accepted into a named baseline, superseded baseline member, withdrawn.
- Progress: not started, in progress, blocked, complete against defined work criteria; progress is separate from technical acceptance.
- Verification/validation/acceptance: retain assurance evidence and authority defined in 8I-41.

A deliverable being issued does not mean it is approved for construction. A client review response does not automatically establish technical verification. A document can be mature but not accepted; it can be issued for information without being a baseline member. Preserve exact revision and status semantics in all exports and dashboards.

### 8I-43.7. Deliverable lifecycle and revision history

Model each revision as an immutable, traceable version with author, timestamp, change summary, source inputs, review cycle and supersession relation. Draft editing may occur in a working area, but issue packages must point to frozen revision identities. Revisions are not just sequential filenames: support project-specific revision schemes while preserving an internal monotonic identity.

A typical lifecycle is planned → preparation → internal check → interdisciplinary coordination → external/client review → comment resolution → approval/authorization for issue → transmittal. Later issue purposes and as-built states are separate transitions. Withdrawal and supersession must retain the historical record and explain why a revision is no longer current.

Reissue of unchanged content for a different purpose must be represented as a new issue event referencing the same content revision where policy permits, not falsely represented as new technical content. Content change requires a new revision. Define controlled correction/reissue rules and preserve the complete issue history.

### 8I-43.8. Work package and activity contracts

A work package should declare:
- Scope, boundary, inclusion/exclusion and completion criteria.
- Required inputs, prerequisite deliverables and minimum maturity/approval states.
- Expected outputs and associated deliverables.
- Responsible discipline/team, accountable owner and authorized contributors.
- Dependencies, interface obligations and constraints.
- Planned, forecast and actual start/finish dates, duration and calendar.
- Planned/actual effort and resource requirements where supported.
- Risk, assumptions, issues, decisions and action links.
- Evidence required to declare the package complete.
- Change history and baseline membership.

Activity records support scheduling and coordination, but activity completion alone cannot establish work-package acceptance, deliverable approval, design verification or operational release. Completion rules must be explicit and versioned. A package can be administratively complete while a technical deliverable remains under review; the UI must show the distinction.

### 8I-43.9. Schedule and dependency graph

Represent dependencies as typed, directed relations with explicit source and target identities, relation semantics, optional lead/lag, validity, owner and provenance. Candidate schedule relationships include finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish. Support milestones, calendars, working-time rules, constraints and baseline/forecast/actual dates.

Separate:
- Logical technical dependency: one design or calculation requires another output/input.
- Information dependency: a deliverable requires a specific upstream information container or revision.
- Interface dependency: one discipline or supplier owes a defined interface input.
- Organisational assignment: who is responsible for work.
- Physical sequence: actual installation, energisation, testing or commissioning order.
- Contractual dependency: appointment, client decision, purchase order or supplier obligation.

Do not infer one relation from another. A schedule graph may calculate float or critical path only when the schedule engine, calendars, constraints and calculation method are defined and validated. Never fabricate criticality, progress or dates from missing data.

When an upstream revision changes, evaluate only dependent deliverables, work packages, interface records and decisions using declared dependency edges. Preserve the old dependency snapshot and explain why each downstream item is current, potentially affected, stale, under review or explicitly accepted with deviation. A stale engineering output must not be silently treated as approved/current. This is selective impact analysis, not blanket invalidation.

### 8I-43.10. Multidisciplinary interface management

Create an Interface Register with stable interface ID, source/receiving parties, discipline owners, boundary definition, scope, interface control document, required data, assumptions, constraints, due dates, maturity, status, acceptance criteria, evidence and change history.

Initial interface families include:
- Electrical ↔ mechanical: motor ratings, starting duty, torque/speed, driven equipment, loads, earthing and space/access.
- Electrical ↔ instrumentation: instrument power, signal type, isolation, cable, grounding, hazardous-area constraints and marshalling.
- Protection ↔ Control: signal ownership, trip/interlock boundaries, permissives, reset authority, command/feedback semantics and fail-safe behavior; preserve separate execution authorities.
- Electrical ↔ civil/structural: equipment loads, foundation, clearances, cable trenches, earthing grid and building interfaces.
- Piping/process ↔ instrumentation: process connection, tapping, range, impulse line, process conditions, cause/effect and loop requirements.
- Vendor package ↔ project: battery limits, terminal points, data sheets, drawings, signals, utilities, performance guarantees and certified documentation.
- Plant ↔ utility/grid: point of connection, fault levels, protection coordination, metering, telemetry, grid-code and operating constraints.

Interface freeze is a controlled state tied to named revisions and agreed assumptions, not a claim that no later change is possible. Changes after freeze trigger impact assessment and re-coordination. Interface agreement must not override the technical domain's own validation rules.

### 8I-43.11. Reviews, comments and approval workflow

Support internal check, independent discipline check, interdisciplinary review, vendor review, owner/client review and formal approval as distinct review types. Each review cycle records exact deliverable revision, review scope, reviewers, due date, disposition, comments, response owner, response, closure evidence and final decision.

Comments need stable IDs, location/context references, severity/category, originator, responsible responder, due date, response code, status, disposition rationale and links to affected engineering objects. A comment marked closed must have an auditable response and closure authority. Reopened comments retain history. Comment resolution is not itself approval of the deliverable.

Approval authority, quorum, signature requirements, escalation and delegation are project-configurable and must comply with 8I-39 access controls and 8I-41 assurance. Record approval meaning and scope precisely: technical check, owner acceptance, authorization to issue, or baseline approval are not interchangeable.

### 8I-43.12. Transmittal and controlled information exchange

A transmittal is an immutable distribution event/package. It records sender, recipient organisation/person, purpose, issue date/time, exact deliverable IDs and revisions, included attachments, security classification, message, signature/authorization, delivery channel and receipt evidence. Revisions cannot be substituted after issue without creating a new transmittal or controlled amendment.

The transmittal record must preserve what was actually sent, to whom, for what purpose and under which authorization. A receipt confirms delivery/receipt, not technical acceptance. A transmittal does not automatically approve a design or alter a project baseline. External CDE/document-management systems may remain authoritative for distribution; GridForge should integrate through explicit exchange contracts rather than assume it is the universal CDE.

### 8I-43.13. Vendor and supplier data management

Provide a Vendor Document Requirement List (VDRL) or equivalent register, linked to procurement package and technical scope. Capture required vendor documents, responsible supplier, required submission stage, planned/actual dates, review cycle, status, comments, deviations, certified revision and affected equipment/interface references.

Vendor data classes include general arrangement, certified drawings, datasheets, performance curves, terminal plans, wiring diagrams, I/O lists, protection/control documentation, test procedures, FAT records, manuals, spare parts and as-built documents. Vendor submissions enter a staging/review process: validate identity, units, completeness, schema, revision, applicability and interface consistency before acceptance into project engineering data.

Vendor-provided models or settings must not automatically overwrite canonical equipment models, topology, Control logic or Protection settings. Store vendor source, received revision, review disposition, adopted values and deviations distinctly. Supplier approval is not equivalent to GridForge engineering validation or final client acceptance.

### 8I-43.14. Procurement, construction and commissioning interfaces

GridForge may produce or exchange technical requisitions, datasheets, specifications, bills of material, material take-offs, approved vendor lists and technical bid evaluation evidence. ERP remains the authority for purchase orders, commercial terms, invoices, inventory and financial commitments unless a separately approved integration contract says otherwise.

Construction interface records may include issued-for-construction deliverables, work-pack references, material status, RFIs, technical queries, field observations, redlines, nonconformances, site instructions and punch-list links. Field information is evidence/proposal until reviewed and reconciled. A redline must not silently mutate an approved design baseline.

Commissioning packages must link to exact approved design baselines, equipment identities, test procedures, inspection records, calibration evidence, protection/control configuration and acceptance criteria from 8I-41. Construction completion, mechanical completion, pre-commissioning, commissioning, energisation authorization and operational handover remain distinct states and authorities. Work-package closure must not bypass safety interlocks or domain release rules.

### 8I-43.15. Engineering maturity and progress measurement

Maturity stages must be configurable by contract, discipline and deliverable class. A generic stage sequence may be used as a starting point, but not imposed on all disciplines. For example, an electrical SLD, protection study, civil foundation drawing, control narrative and vendor certified drawing do not mature through identical technical gates.

Progress should be derived from declared evidence and versioned rules: weighted deliverable milestones, objectively completed work steps, accepted review gates, or other approved measurement method. The rule definition, weights, denominator, exclusions, scope baseline and calculation timestamp must be visible. Do not allow arbitrary subjective percentages to masquerade as measured engineering progress.

Keep separate metrics for physical work completion, engineering production progress, deliverable review/approval progress, scope maturity, interface closure, vendor data readiness, construction readiness and commissioning readiness. Planned, forecast and actual dates are separate values. A deliverable marked 100% complete administratively may still be rejected or technically unverified; dashboards must make this explicit.

### 8I-43.16. Resource and workload governance

Support assignment of work to discipline teams, roles, named authorised users and external organisations. Resource planning may include competency/qualification requirements, availability, planned effort, forecast effort, workload and capacity. Competency evidence and authorisation are separate: assignment does not prove qualification or confer approval authority.

Workload views should show assumptions and source data. Avoid deriving employee performance, productivity or disciplinary conclusions from crude task counts, time entries or progress percentages. Sensitive personnel information requires access control and data minimisation. Detailed payroll, HR records and contractor commercial terms remain outside the engineering execution model.

### 8I-43.17. Engineering change, scope change and commercial variation

Support distinct intake types: engineering change request, design change, technical query, field change, vendor deviation, standards deviation, scope change and contractual/commercial variation. Each has its own origin, authority, evaluation and approval path. A technical change may cause a commercial variation, but the two are not the same record and one must not automatically approve the other.

Impact assessment should consider technical correctness, safety, Protection/Control behavior, topology, studies, equipment, signals, drawings, deliverables, interfaces, procurement, construction, commissioning, cost, schedule, risk and affected baselines. Record affected objects and revisions, alternatives, assumptions, approvals, implementation evidence and verification/revalidation.

Accepted changes create new controlled revisions/baseline relationships. Rejected or deferred changes remain in history with rationale. Emergency field changes require explicit emergency authority, containment and subsequent review/reconciliation; urgency is not permission for untracked mutation.

### 8I-43.18. Risk, assumption, issue, decision and action governance

Provide linked registers with stable IDs and typed semantics:
- Risk: uncertain event and probability/impact, cause, consequence, owner, mitigation, residual exposure and review date.
- Assumption: proposition relied upon, source, owner, validation method and expiry/trigger.
- Constraint: imposed limit or obligation, authority, scope and evidence.
- Issue: present condition requiring resolution, owner, severity, due date and impact.
- Decision: question, alternatives, rationale, decision authority, participants, evidence, effective date and supersession links.
- Action: specific accountable task, due date, completion evidence and closure authority.

Technical decisions should be immutable once approved; corrections and replacements create superseding records. Link decisions to affected domain objects, deliverables, interfaces, risks and baselines. A risk status is not a technical validation result. Risk acceptance must identify the authorized risk owner and residual-risk rationale.

### 8I-43.19. Engineering quantities, estimates and cost boundary

Material take-offs and engineering quantities should be reproducible from an identified source revision and calculation method. Record quantity type, unit, rounding, exclusions, allowances, maturity, uncertainty, source model/drawing revision and manual adjustments. Distinguish calculated, measured, vendor-quoted and manually estimated quantities.

Cost estimates may consume engineering quantities and external pricing, but cost precision must not exceed the maturity and uncertainty of the input data. Estimate classification, contingency and accuracy bands are project-, sector- and jurisdiction-specific; they require explicit methodology and cannot be inferred from a generic label. Budget, actual cost, cash flow, commitment, invoice and commercial forecast remain ERP/project-controls authority unless explicitly integrated.

### 8I-43.20. External systems and data integration

Potential integrations include scheduling tools, document/CDE platforms, ERP/procurement, vendor portals, BIM/CAD platforms, issue trackers, field systems and commissioning systems. For every data class, define the authoritative system, GridForge's role (owner, consumer, producer, cache or reference), stable external ID, mapping, schema/version, synchronization direction, update frequency, conflict policy, idempotency, provenance and error/reconciliation process.

Do not mirror an entire external platform merely to create a dashboard. Imported data must be staged, validated and attributed to its source revision/time. Synchronization failure must be visible and must not silently substitute stale data. Human review is required where imported values could alter engineering truth, approval status or baseline membership.

### 8I-43.21. Dashboards and engineering execution workspaces

Candidate workspaces:
- Project overview: scope, milestones, baseline, key risks, decisions and readiness.
- WBS explorer: typed breakdown views and cross-mappings.
- Deliverable register: filtering by discipline, system, status, maturity, revision, owner and due date.
- Work package board: scope, dependencies, owners, dates, evidence and blockers.
- Schedule/dependency view: typed dependency graph, critical path only when supported by a validated schedule calculation.
- Interface register/board: boundary, parties, due dates, freeze state and unresolved issues.
- Review inbox: assignments, aging, comment responses, overdue reviews and approval queues.
- Transmittal builder/history: exact issue package and receipt evidence.
- Vendor data workspace: VDRL, submissions, deviations and certified-data status.
- Change/risk/decision registers: impact and ownership.
- Construction/commissioning readiness: exact baseline and evidence prerequisites.

Every aggregate must expose its definition, source, timestamp, scope denominator and stale-data state. Avoid unexplained red/amber/green badges or a single overall progress score that hides discipline-specific blockers. Users must be able to navigate from dashboard metric to underlying work item, deliverable revision, engineering object and evidence.

### 8I-43.22. Security, audit and records retention

Apply role- and project-scoped access, external-party isolation, least privilege, segregation of duties, confidentiality labels, approval authority, secure transmittals and immutable audit events consistent with 8I-39. Audit status transitions, assignments, review decisions, comment responses, baseline membership, imports/exports, signature events and administrative overrides.

Retention, legal hold, export and deletion policies are project/contract/jurisdiction-specific. Preserve provenance and integrity for issued deliverables and transmittals. Do not equate an application audit log with a legally valid electronic signature; signature assurance and legal effect require explicit policy, identity proofing and applicable jurisdictional review.

### 8I-43.23. UX and accessibility requirements

The execution UI should support multiple useful views of the same linked data without creating duplicate sources of truth. Provide:
- Project landing page with actionable engineering status, not generic executive decoration.
- Hierarchical WBS navigation with clear hierarchy type and mapping.
- Dense but accessible deliverable tables with saved filters, bulk actions subject to authorization, visible revision/status axes and keyboard navigation.
- Work-package detail with inputs, outputs, dependencies, evidence and completion criteria.
- Interface board with owner/recipient, boundary, data obligations and freeze/change state.
- Review inbox with comment context and response history.
- Transmittal composition that freezes exact content revisions before issue.
- Schedule and dependency views that remain navigable at large project scale.
- Clear distinction between draft, submitted, reviewed, accepted, approved, issued, superseded and baseline states.

Use accessible names, keyboard operability, visible focus, non-colour status cues, scalable layouts and predictable navigation. Avoid status icons without textual meaning. Large registers require virtualisation/pagination, server-side filtering where applicable and bounded query behavior. Preserve user workspace preferences separately from canonical project state.

### 8I-43.24. Candidate standards and reference framework

Candidate references for further applicability and edition verification:
- ISO 21502:2020, Project, programme and portfolio management — Guidance on project management. ISO currently marks the 2020 edition for revision; ISO/CD 21502 was registered as a committee draft on 2026-09-25. Treat the draft as under development, not a published replacement.
- ISO 10006:2017, Quality management — Guidelines for quality management in projects. ISO records it as confirmed current in 2023.
- ISO 10007:2017, Quality management — Guidelines for configuration management; coordinate with the baseline/change governance in 8I-41.
- ISO 19650 series, information management using BIM; use relevant parts for information requirements, information production, review, delivery and handover where the project scope is BIM-related. Do not assume every GridForge deliverable is a BIM model or that ISO 19650 alone defines the complete engineering project workflow.
- ISO 9001 quality-management principles and project-specific quality plans; distinguish QMS compliance from deliverable approval.
- PMI WBS and project-controls guidance, AACE recommended practices and scheduling/cost-estimating references as informative methods, not automatically normative requirements.
- Discipline-specific IEC/ISO/IEEE/ISA and BIS-adopted standards must be verified against project jurisdiction, contract, edition, amendments and applicability using the standards governance in 8I-25.

No statement of BIS adoption, legal applicability, certification, contractual compliance or conformance is made by this research section. Primary reference pages reviewed: ISO 21502:2020 and ISO/CD 21502 status (https://www.iso.org/standard/74947.html and https://www.iso.org/standard/95368.html); ISO 10006:2017 status (https://www.iso.org/standard/70376.html); ISO 19650 information-management concepts (https://www.iso.org/obp/ui?_escaped_fragment_=iso%3Astd%3Aiso%3A19650%3A-1%3Adis%3Aed-2%3Av1%3Aen). PMI WBS material was used as informative practice only (https://www.pmi.org/learning/library/developing-elaborating-work-breakdown-structures-7241).

### 8I-43.25. Candidate acceptance scenarios

- UI-ACC-PROJ-01: Create an engineering project with explicit scope, contract/package references and governance policy.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-02: Maintain project, plant/system, work, deliverable and organisational breakdowns independently.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-03: Map one deliverable to multiple systems and work packages without duplicating its identity.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-04: Change a display code while preserving stable project, WBS and deliverable identities.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-05: Create a work package with scope, inputs, outputs, owner, dependencies and evidence-based completion criteria.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-06: Maintain deliverable metadata, revisions, purpose and separate lifecycle/maturity/review/baseline states.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-07: Prevent an issued-for-information document from being represented as approved for construction.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-08: Record a review cycle against an exact immutable deliverable revision.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-09: Track comments, responses, reopenings and closure authority without losing history.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-10: Generate a transmittal containing exact revisions and preserve recipient, purpose, authorization and receipt evidence.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-11: Represent typed schedule dependencies and distinguish technical, information, organisational and physical-sequence relationships.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-12: Recalculate schedule indicators only when calendar, constraints and schedule method are defined; otherwise show unavailable.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-13: Change an upstream engineering revision and identify only declared downstream dependencies as potentially affected.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-14: Create an interface record with boundary, parties, required data, owner, due date and acceptance criteria.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-15: Freeze an interface against exact revisions and route post-freeze changes through impact review.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-16: Stage vendor submissions, validate them and record review/deviation without overwriting canonical engineering data.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-17: Link procurement technical outputs to external procurement records without claiming ERP authority.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-18: Reconcile field redlines as proposals and preserve the approved baseline until authorized change acceptance.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-19: Link commissioning readiness to exact approved design revisions and assurance evidence.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-20: Calculate progress from a versioned evidence/weighting rule and expose the denominator and source evidence.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-21: Display production progress, technical maturity, review status and acceptance independently.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-22: Record engineering change, vendor deviation and commercial variation as distinct linked records.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-23: Show a dashboard metric's definition, timestamp, source and drill-down path to the underlying evidence.
- UI-ACC-PROJ-24: Enforce project-scoped permissions, segregation of duties and audit history for external-party review and approval.

### 8I-43.26. Open architectural decisions

1. Define the intended V3 engineering-project scope: engineering execution only, or selected project-controls capabilities beyond engineering deliverables.
2. Decide whether GridForge owns a native deliverable register and transmittal service or integrates with an external document/CDE platform as primary authority.
3. Define canonical identity and numbering rules for projects, packages, WBS nodes, work packages, activities, deliverables, revisions and interfaces.
4. Define supported breakdown structures and mapping cardinalities; decide which structures are mandatory for initial release.
5. Define project-configurable lifecycle, maturity, review, issue-purpose and baseline state machines by discipline and deliverable class.
6. Define the first scheduling capability boundary: dependency register only, deterministic schedule engine, or integration with external scheduling systems.
7. Define dependency semantics, calendars, lead/lag, constraints, critical-path and float calculation requirements.
8. Define evidence-based progress measurement methods and approval authority for weighting rules.
9. Define review/approval authority matrices, electronic-signature requirements and segregation-of-duties policies by project.
10. Define transmittal authority and integration with CDE/document-management systems.
11. Define interface freeze semantics and the required discipline-specific interface data schemas.
12. Define vendor document workflows and which supplier data can be adopted into canonical engineering models.
13. Define construction/commissioning interface depth and explicit exclusions from contractor execution management.
14. Define resource planning scope while avoiding unnecessary employee surveillance or HR data duplication.
15. Define risk/decision/action taxonomy and relationship to existing diagnostics, assurance and change-control systems.
16. Define cost-estimate and quantity take-off scope versus external ERP/project-controls authority.
17. Define data ownership, conflict resolution, synchronization and offline collaboration for all external integrations.
18. Define retention, legal hold, confidentiality and electronic signature requirements by jurisdiction and contract.
19. Verify current BIS adoptions, national annexes and contractual applicability for all standards used in project templates.
20. Define acceptance evidence and performance targets for very large deliverable registers, WBS trees, dependency graphs and review queues.

### 8I-43.27. UI/UX gate impact

This section impacts UI-GATE-02 (project/session and persistent project context), UI-GATE-03 (diagnostics for stale inputs, blocked work, failed imports and review exceptions), UI-GATE-04 (accessibility and dense engineering workflows), UI-GATE-05 (large-register and dependency-view performance), UI-GATE-06 (cross-domain identity, revision and evidence traceability) and UI-GATE-07 (scope, sequencing and product boundaries). All gates remain open pending approved decisions, representative workflows and acceptance evidence.

### 8I-43.28. Frozen V2 invariants and migration boundary

Preserve the frozen V2 architecture: Core owns electrical/domain truth; Application owns commands, services and controlled mutation; UI is projection and interaction; plugins use public contracts and Application services; Protection and Control remain separate execution authorities; the established V2 project package contract remains unchanged.

V3 execution records may reference domain objects, revisions, deliverables and assurance evidence but must not become alternate authorities for topology, measurements, Protection decisions, Control execution, solver results, asset condition or commissioning acceptance. Project-management plugins must not mutate Core directly. External ERP, CDE, scheduling and vendor systems must integrate through explicit contracts with source authority and provenance.

No change to V2 main, existing project archive schema or frozen architecture is authorized by this research entry.

### 8I-43.29. Research disposition

Research-only proposal. No implementation, tests, CI, benchmarks, runtime validation, standards conformity assessment, BIS adoption verification or certification was performed. V2 main remains unchanged. UI-GATE-02 through UI-GATE-07 remain open. The status of ISO 21502:2020 and ISO/CD 21502 is recorded as observed on 2026-11-04 and must be rechecked before normative use.


## 8I-44. Proposed V3 Blender-inspired engineering workbench, context-first interaction and at-a-glance data architecture (2026-11-04)

### 8I-44.1. Objective and design thesis

Make GridForge a professional engineering workstation in which the engineer keeps the primary engineering document visible while reaching relevant tools, properties, object hierarchy, linked data, diagnostics, results and commands with minimal navigation. The target is not visual imitation of Blender and not unrestricted panel proliferation. The target is a coherent, discoverable and customizable workbench that reduces repetitive navigation and keeps engineering context visible.

Adapt Blender's strongest principles: workspaces/screens contain editor areas; editor areas contain regions; each editor has a recognizable identity, header and local tools; workspaces are task-oriented arrangements rather than separate databases; active-tool settings are close to the tool; search, context menus and quick favorites accelerate discovery; status guidance explains the current interaction; layouts are customizable. Blender's published interface guidance describes screen/area/region hierarchy and non-overlapping, non-blocking interaction. These principles should be adapted, not copied literally: https://developer.blender.org/docs/features/interface/human_interface_guidelines/paradigms/ ; https://developer.blender.org/docs/features/interface/human_interface_guidelines/editors/ ; https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/dev/interface/index.html .

### 8I-44.2. Three-level workbench hierarchy

Adopt three conceptual levels:
1. Workspace/Screen: named task arrangement, active engineering context, editor layout, visible panels and workspace-specific shortcuts.
2. Editor Area: replaceable editor instance such as SLD, Control Ladder, Protection function/coordination, Study configuration/results, equipment/data browser, report, timeline or diagnostics.
3. Editor Regions: header, toolbar/tool shelf, main view, contextual sidebar, Inspector/Properties, lists/channels, timeline, status/help strip and editor-local menus.

A workspace is not a document, project, discipline domain or plugin. One workspace can contain multiple editor areas. A document can be shown in multiple views where supported. Workspace layout is presentation state, not a second engineering database.

### 8I-44.3. Global application frame

Candidate shell anatomy:
- Top application bar: project/document identity, save/sync state, global command/data search, workspace tabs, user/workspace controls and high-priority project warnings.
- Main menu: stable application commands organized by project, edit, view, document, engineering, tools, window/workspace and help.
- Workspace strip: task workspaces with visible active state and keyboard navigation.
- Editor header: editor identity, active document, local mode/tool, view controls, editor-type selector and context selectors.
- Left region: collapsible Project Explorer/Outliner and contextual Tool Shelf; tabbed or split where useful.
- Central editor grid: one or more split editor areas, with tabs and optional secondary windows.
- Right region: contextual Inspector/Properties with sections for object data, active tool, relations, configuration, validation and provenance.
- Bottom region: collapsible Diagnostics, messages, results, activity/timeline, command history or task progress.
- Status/help strip: active tool's next action, modifier hints, selection summary, coordinate/grid/snap state, operation progress and actionable warnings.

The central engineering document should receive the largest default screen allocation. Panels should not crowd it. Frequently needed controls remain one action or shortcut away; advanced data is progressively disclosed.

### 8I-44.4. Task-oriented workspace presets

Initial preset candidates:
- Project: overview, project explorer, deliverables, recent documents, validation summary, work packages and readiness.
- Electrical / SLD: large SLD editor, electrical equipment/tool shelf, system Outliner, selected-equipment Inspector, connection/snap controls and topology diagnostics.
- Protection: relay/function tree, settings Inspector, measurement/input provenance, zone context, decision trace and TCC/coordination editor when supported.
- Control: Ladder/function-block editor, canonical component palette, I/O and signal browser, component/port Inspector, cycle status, interlocks and execution trace.
- Instrumentation & Signals: instrument/loop/channel tree, signal routing editor, measurement quality/freshness Inspector, calibration and acquisition status.
- Studies: study case/configuration, assumptions and input snapshot, solver options, progress, results, plot/table editors, comparison and report.
- Commissioning / Operations Trace: equipment/functional location browser, approved baseline, test records, alarms/SOE/historian references, command-feedback trace and handover evidence.
- Reports & Exchange: report/document browser, source revision/provenance, templates, import staging, export profiles and transmittals.

Presets are starting layouts, not role restrictions. Users may customize, duplicate and save layouts. Unsupported capabilities must be visibly unavailable with an explanation; a workspace must not imply that every listed feature is implemented.

### 8I-44.5. Editor type system and lifecycle

Every editor area has a visible editor-type selector and stable editor identity. Switching an area from SLD to table/plot changes the view, not the canonical project or domain object. Support split, join, close, duplicate view, move to new window and tab operations with clear previews and safe lifecycle behavior.

Editor declarations include editor ID/version, owning domain, accepted document/object types, selection/context capabilities, supported tools/actions, header/region contributions, property and diagnostic read models, keyboard context, persistence policy, activation/deactivation/disposal and plugin contract version. Do not use generic fallback editors that visually imply unsupported semantics; provide a clear read-only details view where no dedicated editor exists.

### 8I-44.6. Shared context model

Use a typed context model for active project/revision, workspace, editor, document/revision, domain/mode, active tool/lifecycle, selection, pinned Inspector target, local browse context, study/run/result/time context and current operation/diagnostics.

Distinguish active context from local browse context. Inspecting a different Outliner/search result must not silently change canvas selection. A pinned Inspector target remains pinned until unpinned or unavailable. Clearly label pinned, historical, remote or non-active context. Selection changes update contextual panels through typed read models; they must not cause document replacement, unexpected tool cancellation or domain mutation. Multi-selection shows common values and per-object differences, and does not flatten incompatible types into a generic edit form.

### 8I-44.7. Contextual Inspector / Properties editor

Treat the Inspector as a primary engineering editor, not a narrow property grid. Keep it discoverable in a stable right region and optionally openable/pinnable in another editor area.

Candidate context-dependent sections:
- Item: designation, type, identity, hierarchy and engineering summary.
- Configuration: editable domain-owned settings and typed forms.
- Tool: active tool options and next-operation settings.
- Electrical: terminals, topology references, ratings, phase and characteristics.
- Signals: measurement bindings, units, quality, timestamps, calibration and provenance.
- Protection: functions, inputs, settings, dependencies, blocked/stale state and decision history.
- Control: component properties, ports, signal semantics, bindings and execution state.
- Studies: case inputs, assumptions and result references.
- Relations: connected objects, dependencies, drawings, packages and cross-domain links.
- Validation: findings, severity, source, resolution and navigation.
- History: revision, change provenance, draft/accepted/historical values and audit references.

Show only applicable sections. Use domain metadata for type, unit, constraints, description, default provenance, edit policy and commit semantics. Provide search within properties, collapsible groups, favorites, visible draft/modified state and a compact identity header. Advanced fields remain searchable without crowding common tasks. Do not create a universal untyped property bag.

### 8I-44.8. Tool Shelf and canonical tool registry

Provide a consistent editor-local Tool Shelf adjacent to the canvas. Each tool descriptor declares stable ID, domain/editor compatibility, category, icon, label, tooltip, shortcut, cursor/gizmo, supported object types, lifecycle, repeat/sticky policy, configuration schema, cancellation behavior, accessibility metadata and availability reason.

Use hierarchical groups and searchable categories. Tool buttons need recognizable icons and accessible labels; icon-only mode is optional, not the only discovery method. Tool groups expose alternatives without repeated navigation to a distant palette. Active tool state is obvious; settings appear in header and Active Tool properties.

A tool is available only if its complete path is supported: activation, preview, apply/commit, validation, undo/recovery, deactivation and persistence where relevant. Capability declarations must agree across Core semantics, Application commands, persistence and editor projection. This addresses the capability drift class in open issue #1032.

### 8I-44.9. One-shot, repeat, sticky and chained tools

Support explicit tool policies:
- One-shot: operation ends after one successful placement.
- Repeat: remains active after each successful placement.
- Sticky: remains active until explicitly cancelled or switched.
- Chained: continues a sequence such as multi-point wire/route construction.
- Modal: temporary constrained interaction with explicit start/commit/cancel.

Choose defaults by engineering risk and editor semantics. Repeated placements create distinct domain identities and never reuse preview IDs. After placement, users can continue, change parameters, switch tools or return to selection. Escape behavior is documented at every operation stage. Show a visible repeat/sticky state; never leave an invisible active tool. This directly addresses repetitive one-shot workflow concerns in #815.

### 8I-44.10. Global command and data search

Provide an application-wide command/search palette inspired by Blender's F3 search, but with GridForge-specific typed and permission-aware results. Search commands, operations, editors/workspaces, tools, properties, project objects by tag/ID/type/property, documents/sheets/studies/results/reports, diagnostics/alarms, help and shortcuts.

Results show action/object/context, destination editor, shortcut, availability and disabled reason. Filters separate Commands, Tools, Objects, Documents, Diagnostics and Help. Ranking may favor current context and recency but must not hide valid results.

Search is discovery and dispatch, never a bypass. Commands still follow Controller → Command → Application → Core, authorization, validation, transaction, confirmation and audit. Destructive, safety-significant and external-dispatch actions retain safeguards. Do not expose hidden debug operations to ordinary users. Candidate shortcut F3 is subject to centralized cross-platform keymap/conflict review. Blender search reference: https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/4.4/interface/operators.html .

### 8I-44.11. Outliner and engineering data browser

Provide searchable project hierarchy views for plant/system/equipment; electrical network and SLD documents/sheets; Protection relay/functions; Control programs/components/rungs; instruments/loops/channels/signals; study cases/runs/results; reports/deliverables/assurance records.

These are projections over authoritative objects, not independent editable trees. Search/filter by tag, stable ID, type, system, status, owner, revision, domain and supported metadata. Support expand/collapse, multi-select, selection synchronization, reveal-in-editor, focus, pin, copy identity/reference, show relations and open properties.

A tree selection reveals the object in its owning editor when a valid projection exists. Cross-domain objects open in their owning editor or a read-only contextual view. Do not infer visual connectivity from names or proximity.

### 8I-44.12. Context menus and Quick Favorites

Right-click menus are object-, editor-, selection- and state-aware. Candidate actions: inspect properties, reveal in Outliner, open owning document, navigate to terminal/channel/function, show connected/related objects, copy tag/ID, create supported association, isolate/highlight, fit selection, add annotation, view history and view diagnostics.

Only show valid operations. Disabled actions may show a reason; unsupported actions must not appear functional. Context menus are not the only keyboard/assistive route.

Users may pin frequent commands, tools and panel actions in Quick Favorites. Favorites are scoped global/workspace/editor, searchable and editable. They are shortcuts to canonical commands, not duplicate implementations or a permission layer.

### 8I-44.13. Tool settings and last-operation feedback

Tool settings appear in the editor header/tool settings region and Inspector Active Tool section, synchronized to one tool configuration. Parameters affecting the next operation are distinct from settings for an already completed operation.

An optional last-operation panel must state whether changing a parameter re-runs a new operation, edits an uncommitted draft or issues a new command. Do not imply that an accepted engineering command can be retroactively edited.

Placement/connection previews show snap target identity, compatibility status, coordinate/grid state and commit/cancel instructions. A visual snap is only a candidate until the owning domain/Application command confirms the semantic relationship. Protection/Control previews cannot dispatch live actions merely because the user is configuring a workspace.

### 8I-44.14. Contextual status/help strip
